LADIES' LETTER..

&EY DEAR NELLIE, After a long run the sailor-hat seems to be passing out of favour and other shapes are very frequently seen. The sailor-hat is very useful for a drive, boating and cycling, but not for many other purposes for which these hats are used. They have not, however, altogether disappeared. The newest sailor-hats have wide brims and rather high crowns, tnd have for trimmings bows of glac6 edged with a narrow line of fancy straw-plait. The sun-hat with straw crown and brim composed of overlapping kilted frills of muslin or gauze is still in vogue for river wear, but it is not well suited to withstand see-breezes and sprays. The prettiest hats seen this season have been the big ones, wide at the sides and dipping down in front and behind, trimmed with masses of roses.

A lady was wearing the other afternoon a dress of most 'becoming hue. If I tried to describe it I should say that the bodice is most becomingly arranged with a tucked vest and collar band of lelicate green batiste and lace applique, the deep- pointed collar of lace piped with green falling over an under-collar of white embroidered muslin. If you are not in love with the dress already, you most certainly will be if you could see it in its variously coloured reality, and crown it with a most becoming and picturesque hat of rush straw trimmed with shaded roses and a chic touch of black velvet.

The new light summer skirts are all closely gathered into the wasitband, yet another return to a fashion of the sixties. The gathers of the moment are unlike their predecessors of thirty-five years since in one particular. Whereas the wearers were contented with two rows in those days, five or six are now considered necessary. Robe dresses cif? not lend themselves to fulness at the waist, and now that gathers have come in for thin dresses they are likely, later on, to come into fashion for thicker ones. The fulness gives rather a lumpy look to figures which one has been accustomed to see invested in ithe tightest and plaintest of closely-fitting skirts, but to this the eye will soon become habituated, and the five rows of gathers will soon be associated with all that is smart. Those muslin gowns are in great vogue on the river. Batiste, too, is made in the same way, with ,hardly any goring, the whole fulness being dis- posed of in the gathers.

Substantial frocks intended for girls above nine years of age are made of cashmere, thin cloth, or serge, and the skirts are often finely pleated and stitched all round the top, the full bodices being pleated to correspond, and having almost invariably a deep collar—square, rounded, or vandyked—a smart little -pointed or heart-shaped vest, and a folded belt with ornamental buckle. A pretty little dress may be made of electric-blue face cloth and the collar made of ecru lace over scarlet silk, with a vest of tucked t;cru muslin. The belt in this case might be either scarlet or blue, accord- ing to taste. A skirt of blue serge, ornamented with several rows of stitching round the hem, and a square-cut coat with similar stitchings round all its edges, form a most I:seful costume, and can be worn with a variety of shirts and blouses. Linen or drill collars, stitchod, or trimmed with embroidery or lace, provide a smart fiuish to a plain coat, and, with the aid of a good pattern, they are not difficult to manage. Many of my cyclist friends prefer flowery hats to the ,:mple sailor variety, except when the weather is ill one of its variable moods. The neat bolero, with a dainty front, is still the accepted costume. Fluttering muslin sleeves are not regarded as sea-sonahle, while showers are so fre- quent and "0 heavy as they have been of late. or are white dresses much favoured, on account of the copious mud. The bright weather that came with July has brought out the coolest of zephyrs and the lightest of crinoline hats, rose-crowned, spin- ning past on the nimble wheel. The great majority of bicycle skirts are stone-coloured, dust-coloured, fawn, or covert coating. Navy blue serge seems to be quite neglected for the moment, both by wheelwomen and. river girls, as compared with its immense popularity a couple of years ago, when it was almost a livery tor those who favoured out- door pursuits. Khaki cloth, dropped by the million, has a steadily increasing sale among the well-dressed for travelling costumes and country wear. Pale blue and pa.le green arc usually selected to go with it, as the front or shirt, worn with the bolero. Red is scarcely ever chosen for this purpose. Many of the skirts are unlined, or, if lined, they are made loose from the underskirt. Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

Her Majesty's daughters set an excellent example at the Royal Garda, Party, with regard to the length of their sktrts.These just reached the ground an.l no more. The Queen,it is well-kuown, has the greatest detestation of the long skirt, for outdoor wear, and few of her de- scendents venture to wear one in her presence. There are signs that the long skirt, save for ind9or wear,when it is far more becoming and graceful than tbe shert variety will vanish with the coining autumn. Tailors are building the majority of their early autumn gowns to clear the ground, an item indeed to rejoice over. The Shah, now shortly expected in this country, is generally associated in the public mind, as rejoining ie boundless treasures. So much was this the case when the late ehah first came to this country, that it was popularly supposed that he could give away diamonds and emeralds by the scuttleful, and not miss them. All those notions were of course greatly eiaggerated,though it is no doubt true that the Shah could make a greater show of precious stones and valuablt s than any other Sovereign or Court in the worl3. The gold service at Windsor Castle is supposed to be worth about £2,000,000,h= the Peacock Throve belong- ing to the Shah, is alone worth very much more than that. The frame where it is not of gold, is entirely of silver, and all over it is encrusted with diamonds and other jewels. The rig and pillow which belong to it are also fringed with amethysts and pearls, and altogether it is probably the most costly ornameat that the mind of man bas ever conceived.'

Since hotel and railway thieves have become so ex- pert,many,:wealthy women leave their valuable jewellery with their bankers, and have a certified copy in cheap imitation for ordinary purposes of wear. No doubt this is a wise proceAling, thouzh it seems to reduce the real articles to the level of being little else than a useless encumbrance. It is v.!.ry much like those people who live in " V.lladom," and strictly preserve a best room" only to be entered upon high days and holidays. They shut themselves off from what is, in most cases, the best room in the house, paying rent and taxes for it and taking vast pains to keep it nice, and perhaps only making any use of it at rare intervals, few and far be- tween. This is a great mistake when carried to such extremes. Of course no one possessing valuable jiwellery would wear anything but a certified copy of it, but the practice of wearing sham imitations would seem to bring the wearing of ornaments into disrepote. If titled women do not miad wearing sham articles there • is of course nothing to prevent those people doing the same who have no corresponding real ones at their bankers or elsewhere.

Quite the last event of] the London season will be Lady Randolph Churchill's wedding, which is fixed to take place on the 213 h. Despite the fact that society people are rapidly leaving town the crush will he enormous, and it is quite certain that popular interest in the event will eclipse anything of the kind witnessed this season: It is understood that Lady Randolph Churchill will continue to be known by her present name.which is se familiar to the public. She will, of course, become Mrs. Cornwallis West, but it would be a thousand pities foe Lady Randolph to sink her identity, by sharing the same name as her mother-it-law. Her own fortune is in no way affected by her marriage with Mr. Cornwal'is West. Lady Randolph will retain her life interest in the £70,000 or £BO.OOO which her dis- tinguished husband left behind,and eventually this will pass to her two sons, in such proportions as she &lady decide, The marriage of Wes Amelia Kiiisner, the celebrated miniature painter, came as a surprise, the majority of her vast circle of friends knowing nothing of her engage- ment until it was over Wedding presents however, have "rained" upon the happy pair since their marriage became known, tine especially splendid gift taking tbe form of a beautiful howe in New York, fully furnished and containing many .eicpisite art treasures. By the WirAsor fire in New York, NiS9 Kiissner, or rather Mrs. DJ Pont Coudert as Yee must now eerie her. was a great loser. She had a permanent set of rooms there, which she furnished after her own taste with many art treasures, her small picture gallery including works by M le, and Puvia de Cheyennes. Just before she left tor Russia, Miss liii4sner hail the rooms entirely redecorated, leaving a great many yak's oles there. Her mother-in-law's present will go far towards helping her to forget a loss tor which she has always felt a keen regret. Mrs. Coudert has painted many Royal folks, including the Prince ot Wales, and the Czarina of Russia. and nearly all our " beauties "—Her miniatures are most exquisitely palated,and some day will be worth fortunes.

Wedding presents nowadays, take many and various forms, but two bestowed upon Nliis Clara Butt, now Mrs. Kennerley Rumford, were decidedly out of the u.tual run altogther• These tack the shape of wedding cakes, one consisting of three tiers, and standing six *rd a half feet high. By the way, the P,srmaster- General of New Zsaland has issued stringent rules against the transmission of wedding cake except in tin boxes. He says that when sent in cardboard, or In plper packets it encourages the presence of rats in post offices, and rats spread the plague. All this is doubtless very true, but, wedding cake in tin boxes sounds impossible. Who could appreciste this delicate symbol if it reached one in such a fashion. When the thermometer rises into the eighties, there are occasions when we reflect that the scanty garb of the Ancient Britons was not without its advantages. Such hive been the sentiments of the majority of us, since the hot weather, suddenly stricken with remorse for its unpunctuality, charged down upon us. In the in Ater of heat however, as in many ether crnnections, the important thing is to keep the head cool. If we must drink then we should partake of light and innocu ous beverages only. Further, c'ear soups, fish, salads of every description and unlimited fruit, is the brit dkt to place ourselves upon. In weather such as we have recently experienced, the earth never gets really cool,so that each successive day is likely to he hotter than its prfdecessnr, but on the other hand we grow cash day more accustomed to the heat. - -

White is quite a uniform. When fresh and dainty, nothing is more delightful and becoming. The ancient idea that white is only suitable for very young eirls is quite expledtd, and happily too. But a white gown, soiled, is hopeless. If one cannot see one's way to a gown built of some white fabric paving frequent visits to the dry cleaner, the wisest plan is to indulge in a painted or print( d muslinonany of which with the occ3- sinnal application of a warm iron, can be made to do duty successfully to the last gasp. Barley water is associated with invalids, but as a matter of fact it makes an tx.:ellent beverage for summer use. It is refreshing, healthy and suctsining First wash the bleep thoroughly. The first water poured over and br -neht tn a beil, should also be thrown away. Then add to 2 z;. of pearl barley three pints of clid water, bring it gently to the boil, let it simmer fo- two hours, strain, and add lemon juice and sugar to taste. " MADGE."

div.head: SPEED OF BRITISH CRUISERS.
div.p: THE SPEED OF BRITISH CRUISERS.

" The Admiralty apparently have resolved to s t their house in ordsr," says " Feilden's Magazine." " (he agitation which the Navy L ltgue and the public Press have set in motion to provide the Navy with the latest approved guns has at last borne fruit. Mr G schen, the First Lord, informed the country, at the annual dinter of the Iron and Steel Institute, that shortly the new pat' ern, of 12 in., 92 in., and 6 in. guns would be afloat. And further, a committee, with Lord Rayleigh as chair- man had been appointed, the reference to which was to carry out tria's with a view to asc?rtaining what were the best smokeless propellants for use in existing smalj arms, and further, to report as to whether any modifica- tion in the existing designs was desirable, with a view to developing to the full the powers of any propellant which may ha proposed.

" Then there is the water-tube toiler question. Mr. William Allen and Sir FcrtescuP Flannery still ply questions in the Commons, and the" Pall Mali GazAtto" preaches continually of the innfficiency of the Relit -vino boiler. That there is something wrong with the Belleville boiler there can be no two opinions." After quot;nz in support of these statement+ the results of the trials of the " Higliflyer " and the well-known fact that the " Powerful "took a very long time to return from the Cape, the writer adds the. following strictures "It appears again that the Admiralty is a long way behind other countries in the speed of its cruisers. . In 1898 Messrs. Mitchell and Armstrong launched for the Chinese government the " the fastest cruiser in the world. with an indicated h.p. of 1.700, a displace- ment of 4,300 tons ; she made a speed of 24 knots, aryl her armament is equal to that of the" Sparttate " class, which has only a speed of 204 knots. Thee latter vessels are huge and clumsy, have 11,000 tong displace. ment, and drsw 7 ft. 6 in. more water than the" Ffai- Chi." For the Argentine Republic was built, in 1895, the" Buenos Aires." with 1,000 tons more coal capacity than the" Elai.Chi," and she gave 23•2 knots. is wilt thus be seen that our Admiralty, in design and speed, are quite seven years behind China and the Argentine Republic."

div.head: DEEP SEA WONDERS.
div.p: DEEP SEA WONDERS.
A PRESSURE OF TONS.

To the layman, the reader who has not followed the investik ations of stu.lents of the deep sea, it is difficult o realise how life c.n exist where the prepure is so great that it is (rrripard to a rrain of cars loaded v,ith ,ron bearing down upon a man'4 shooldera, or many toes to the square inch. Neither arc the conditions of life readily understood at a depth where a ray of sunlieht never has reach.d, where etecnal right apparently reigns, where the temperature nearly at n freezing valet, and where,in all prob.bility,a hilerice 1411 profound exists that a sound has never brokeu the quiet of ages. Such a region, finding its extrem, depth in five or six miles, dims not appear to offer many inducements to in- ve..tigatinin ; yet it has beet a most fruitful field, acd the disc ,veries which !lave been matte durin4 tine last few Tears have entirely eh-slued s-ntinleat regarding it. The deep sea, while forbidding and uninviting, has its inhabitants that are well adapted to the strange con- ditions within its borders, where eternal darkness was suppoed to reign. We nave eveey r,a,sori to believe that there is at times a wonderful assemblage of light givers. who illumine am dark, unfathomed ca“ina of the ocean, and change it abysmal regaous into s,Jenes of weird splendour.

div.head: IT 7HB CetAN BED WEBE LAID RARE.
div.p: IT 7HB CetAN BED WEBE LAID RARE.

If the otean bed, wrack] is popularly supposed to occupy three fourths of the world's surface, shr,utd suddenly be laid bare, we should in the main find a duplicate of terrestrial conditions. The bed of the present ocean has at some time been dry laud ; haa been cut by wind and weather, washed into river beds by streams; thrown up by vol- canic action into mountains, or elevated and w pressed by oscillations of the crust. It has undet gone all the changes of the land with which we are familiar, and in a measure resembles it. To make the oce,n b d a reality.we will ark the reader to imagine that be is equipped with a diver's armour capable of resisting pressure, and accompany us into the deep sea. As we descend into the blue depths, we realise that we have entered another world, where,to all intents and purposes, water is the atmosphere. If we entered the Ocean on the P.icific coast from the beach,we would gradually walk down an easy descent for many miles ; and the same is true of the Atlantic. Almost immediately the light fades, so that, %a hen at a ch pth of 500 feet, ,t is comparatively dlik and intensely cold. The deeper we descend, the sunlight gradually fading, until at a depth of a quarter of a mile the daikness is in tense so far as the sun is concernfal.

div.head: ANIMALS STRANGE AND WEIRD
div.p: ANIMALS STRANGE AND WEIRD

In shallow water we have passed through the region of abundant light. Along the shore are schools of por- poises, immense whales that occasionally venture far below the surface, and a number of an -nreathing fish- like animals that are kept near the surface by their structure and requirements. Here are schools of fish— salmon and sardines —and passing is a migrating herd of seals. Deeper we pass and leave them behind, descending to a depth of 1,500 feet in darkness pio- found. An electric light would show a singular chaege• Many of the fish are of gay coloursond could we whisk one to the surface its eyes would be popping from its head, when it arrived, from the sudden change. Strange animals inhabit that regien, and the eciepEr we go the more remarkable they appear, and finally at a mile ar so they fairly compel our admiration. Here are scarlet shrimps, crabs on stilt-like leg.s,othere that are blind, more that carry their own lights, for long aga we saw living stars, moons and comets in this abysmal region that serve a variety of purposes in the economy of nature. Everywhere there is life. Evvry drop of water is alive ; and, standing in this strange re2ioa, at a depth of a mile or so, we find ourselves in a raiuttorns beeeath the sea. •

div.head: STORM BENEATH THE OCEAN.
div.p: A STORM BENEATH THE OCEAN.

All about are countless °News dropping upon us, invisible t) the eye, but so result-prAncing iu the aggre- gate that the raindrops pilo and heap up in such masi,fs that with those that die on the bottom they round off the tops of submarine hills and mountains, fill up the valleys, and the thick gelatinous onzs through which we have walked with so much difficulty is thevisible relult of the rain. In brief, we are in the region of globigerina orze—a condition found in great depths but not always in the greatest. It has been eFtirn ited that if lime- seeTeting organisms are as nifineroul dowa to a depth of 600 feet as tiler are near the surface, there wou?d more than sixteen tons of calcareous shells or ca.b)nr.te of lime in the uppermost 100 fathoms of &very Equare mile of ocean.

The rain storm is the hiling of these cnuotless shells to the bottom. They are ever dying ; the antra,' ii destroyed and the little shell sinks, piling up at the bottom &Ed forming the well-known globigerina ooz,. The incressing si eight grinds up the lower stratum itt, an impslpahle powder and slowly p'les up the bottom, forming a mass which if elevated a'-ove the surf-ice wou'd resemble the chalk cliffs of Dover, which were formed at the bottom of the oonsn in much the sant. way.

div.head: vingaE NO SUNLIGHT PENETRATES
div.p: vingaE NO SUNLIGHT PENETRATES

De3cending into deeper depths, we still find life. Many of the fi43ea sre blind, nearly all have phosphor- escent light,- and their shapes and corms are arr.nge and uncanny. Sunlight does not reach 11..10w 1,000 fathoms; beyond this no plant file t xists, and the various tvrms of life p7ey upon one another. Among the deep-sea fishes especially tire is constant warfare. Assuming that we arc cva king on the ocean bottom at the mpth of over a mile, we move cautiously along in watur icy c-ild,and suddenly are confronted with a bl-z of light and find ourselves in a field of light-give rs, Imagine a cornfield with stalks from two to four feet in height, the tips gleaming with light and waving gently to and fro. Sue) an appeerat,c) the fiel3s of umnellutaria present. Off Sc. Vincent the Ch dlenger d,edged in a fittld Af light-giving gorgonias with stems to feet long. The trawl came up choked with them from a region a mile below the surface, each one emit:ing a vivid, lilac coloured light,

div.head: FOREST OF LIVING LIGHTS.
div.p: FOREST OF LIVING LIGHTS.

Above th;ts forest of living lights strange and weird fishes are passing, wiiich we rec ignise as f,rms that have tY en dredged from great depths by the Challeogar and other bests. Oat, ugly ere& ure dashes by, emitting light from its own body, and. wonder of wonuers ! , we see it seize a fish five times its own bulk and draw itself over it like a glove. Is jiws, by a special arrangeme it, separate, and the mouth is a cavern of india rubber like pessibilities. A similar fish is of a rich black v..lver hue, and as it poises we sre upon it i !head two lary lights. One emits a gollets light, the other throws cot beaut!- ful green rays, which hive aim i hidden meaning ia the economy of nature. B,tne of the, filles s,erai to be titan mouths. -uch is the Eurypharvna or pelieaa fish. fhe mouth i n°3111)114, the bones of the jaw tieing attAc'ie to the skull by movable joints. so that it has enormaus powers of distention. A curious black Mt), group Echinodermata. has its lanterns arranged atiou-, its head ; two are just blow thn oyes, white there are several others at various portions of the head. At a depth of two miles we find the fi,h Bythites, and at three mile 4we find others more remarkable. k hideous snakelike creature is Stornatia, with pointel teen and a row of lights alone its ventral surface like the lie,h s thar are seen in a dark night in the car window as the train dishes alenZ. IN DAVY JONE4'S LOCKER.

Beneath our feet are forms equa.lly weird, th? h blaz.ng with light at every st-p. Here are phosplio es- cent crabs, and seafats that emit golden, green and lilac hues. Blue scintillations coma from sea-pens, others give out gleams of gold and green• evory animal is a liht giver. Som. of trio crab+ are ph ,•- phorescent over the entire surface ; others have th r lights on stalked eyes, while the wry mud that seems to seittillate with light that would appear to ho essefitial features of the deep sea. We might in this walk of the imagination desc-nd to a depth of six miler. beneath the sea and still and life.

In all probability the largest and most rem•irkatla fishes have nct been seen, and e,cape the dre.lee. Many of these strange forms of the abysmal depna are types of extinct forms,and we can only imagine what wonders the deep fel hides. In the Atlantic and Pacific gigan,ie squids from 50 to 75 feet in length are touno, ant glimpaes of strange snake or IN 1-like sharks are auggea- Live of the uncaught mysteries and unae,ll dwellers in deep sea. Am•ing the curious light-givers is a FilNei whieh was caught by Dr. Bennett. It was pi•rfec,iv black.bu*, mitted a strange phosphorescent light whic:l remained come time after the animal's death. Thelirk was placNi in a jar ia the cab'n cf tha vessel and it described as presenting a ghostly appearance, emitting a rich green light almrs'; sufficient to rrad by. In ce.cending ilito 'he intermediate depths, the .11v- fishes and forms that live in the open water attrac our attention. Here is a jelly fith, its disc 6 feet across, i train of tentacles posibly emitting a vivid light and stre'cl,ing away in a na,ze cf brilliant lines for T.l-13a,,t4 100 feet, Such a jally-fish meting through the upper depth a might well ba compared to a great comM,.

div.p: (Copyright. THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
BY JOSEPH HOCKING,
Author of "The Birthright," '!Mistress Nancy Molesworth," "All Men are Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," &c.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Alizon Neville, who belongs to an old Roman Catholic family, pays, for curiosity's sake,, a-secret visit to Tudor Chapel, the Nopconformizt place of worship at Lynford. She hears the new minister, Duncan Rutland, and by chance is thrown across his path The virility of his Protestantism makes her half dis like him. She fears he will do much harm amon the Catholic population in unsettling their beliefs: Events so arrange themselves that at her instigation Father Sheen, her confessor, agrees to meet Duncan for a public debate about Roman Catholicism. In the first debate Rutland easily disposes of his Catholic antagonist. Much chagrined, Alizon un- wittingly encourages some Catholic weavers to trap the young minhiter, so that he shall not appear at the second debate. When she is fully conscious of what is happening, Alizon hastens to save him. She succeeds, and Rutland, who is falling in love with her, is overwhelmingly triumphant at the second debate, but the girl fedi- that she dislikes him more than • ever. Father Sheen. dare not face a third debate. He sends for an eminent Jesuit, Father Ritzoom, who advises him not to appear. Ritzoom has a plan, founded upon Duncan's supposed affec- tion for Alizon, whereby Duncan shall be led to recant his "heresy," join the Church of Rome, and become a priest.
CIIAPTER XI.
AT TILE PRTOP.Y.

On the following Wednesday morning, a letter appeared in the I,ynford Observer, stating that owing to medical advice, Father Sheen had yielded to the wishes of the authorities of his Church, and had decided not to take part in that night's debate. The letter was carefully wortied, and a medical certificate appended, so that to an outsider it would seem as though the priest had, after much per- suasion, foregone a duty which would have yielded him great pleasure. Many jokes were passed in the factories, while many conjectures were offered as to the course things ,would take.

"I thowt Rutland :gave Sheen a 'eadache last Wednesday neat; aw spouse oo's nuan got over it yet," said old Matthy Bray, as he read the letter. "Yi, aw spouse oo'l be sittin' in his armcheer a vinegar cloth tied araand his 'ead," said the man to whom the old wearer spoke. "Weal, aw'm glad aw voated for Rutland comin' to Tudor. Oo's just the man for us." "Yi, and so am I. Some foak seaci as aa oo wilt too young. But aw seed as aa the lad 'ad gotten brains. Tell the., lad, the chap as baits Rutland'll 'ave to geet up middlin' early. Oo'll noan 'ave mich time for breakfast."
"Thotert near right, Maltby; but saint, wot's yon ? "

The two men were on th3ir way to dinner. They had just left the factory, and were passing through the principal street in the town. The object which attracted their attention was a huge placard; announcing that as Father Sheen had declared that he would be unable to take part in the debate, and as nearly two thousand tickets were sold for the same, Mr. Rutland would give a lecture on "The Right of Private Judgment in Religious Matters."

The weavers laughed gleefully as they read it. "00's noan lost much time, Jonas," said Matthy • Bray. "Nay, the lad's made up his mind middlin' quick. Art a baan ? " "Yi, aw am an all ;. aw would'n miss it for summat. Aw doan't think mony people'll stay away 'cause Sheen isn't coming." "Except th' Cathlicks," remarked Jonas. "Thou rt reight. Jonas," said Matthy. 'iCathlicks'll ncan coom to-fleet. All th' same, th" all' 11 be f ull. " •

aw shall geet middlin' early." As the weaver had predicted, the hall was crowded, although no Catholics appeared on the platform, and, as far as could be judged, very few were in the main building. Only a few of the people noticed a dark, clean-shaven man, with large, square features, who sat in the middle of the hall. Except that his face denoted remarkable strength, there seemed no reason for paying him particular attention. He was dressed in dark serge clothes, and his short, double-breasted coat accentuated the broad shoulders, and powerful chest. He spoke no word to anyone, but seemed to observe the character of the meeting closely. When Rutland walked on to the platform, and the people rose en maw to cheer him, not a muscle of his face moved, but his keen, dark eyes were fixed on the young minister, as though he were much interested 10 hint. Through( ut Rutland' address the man noted his every inovethcnt, listened. to every word he uttered, and marked ith evident interest the impression he made upon the audience. The people laughed, cheered, shouted, and became indignant, scornful, and enthusiastic in turn ; but this man never altered the expression of his face. That he was interested no one could doubt; but what he thought of the, eager young speaker who swayed the multitude at will, no one could gather. He was as silent as the Sphinx, and his face was immovable. When the lecture was over a man, who Was sitting next to him, spoke in a friendly way, characteristic of Lancashire people. "Yo're a stranger to Lynford, aw reckon ? " he said.

"Yes," was the answer. "Aw doan know wot th' Cathlicks will say after to-nest," remarked the Lynford man. "Rutland's fairly shewed up the result of priests tryin' to hinder people thinkin' baat religions matters." "He has, indeed," said the stranger.

"That lecture 'll be a reg'lar knock-downer for Father Sheen, an' all th' Cathlicks, won't it ? " The man did not reply, but rose and left the hall, not deigning to listen to the men who got up to propose a vote of thanks to Duncan for the valiant stand he had taken. He walked some distance down the street, when hearing the Town Hall clock chiming, he turned and looked in that direction. . _

"A quarter-past nine," he said. "I shall be in good time." lie went to a cabstand, and entered one of the conveyances. "The Priory," he said, quietly. A little later the cab drew up before the entrance of Lady Neville' old home. Evidently the visitor was expected, for be was immediately ushered into the room where Lady Neville and Alizon sat, together with Father Sheen. "You are back early," said Father Sheen. "Yes, I carne away as soon as Rutland had finished his lecture." "Well, and what was your impression of him, Father Ritzuom ? " asked Lady Neville.

The Jesuit was silent for a few seconds. He looked at the two lathe., and at Father Sheen, as though he wondered what had passed between them during the evening. "I think it is a great pity that a man possessing such talents should remain outside the Church," ho replied. "It is, indeod," remarked Lady Neville ; "but, what can be done with him ? "

"Can't you think? " asked Ritzoom, eyeing the occupants of the room keenly. "I wish 1 could," she replied. It is no use denying the matter: he has struck our Church a heavy blow," remarked Father Sheen, pathetically. Alizon said nothing, but listened eagerly to what was said.
• "Father Ritzoom," said Lady Neville, "I wish you could think of some means whereby the harm he has done could he nullified."

_ "It would be better still if it could be made to render us good service," remarked the Jesuit, quietly. "Yes, yes, of course; but-that seems impossible." "Didn't you think him conceited, pedantic, and --and arrogant to-night, 'Father Ritzoom ? " asked Alizon, somewhat impatiently. "Perhaps, slightly," replied the Jesuit, "but not unduly so. I remembered that he is a young man, and that the applause of the multitude was enough to make him a little—well, over certain." "Was his lecture abier?" asked Father Sheen.

“it was a very dangerous address, a very dangerous address,” was the reply. "It appealed to those qualities which are characteristic of the Anglo-Saxon race." "And they? " asked Alizcm. "They may be all summed up in a word—self- importance. He played upon this, flattered it, fostered it, elorified it. Hie made the ,authority

of Owl's ordained priests a very difficult matter. I should not be surprised if many of Father !Iheen's floc k go astray." —Lin, It s a shame, a shame!" cried Alison, hotly. "Cannot something be done? It makes one long for the power of the Inquisition." "Yes, it helps one to understand some of those deeds which Protestants make so much of. But we are in England, and we are but a weak, struggling people here. We want a new Refoz:-

"And that seems impossible," remarked Lady Neville. "Pardon me, I think not," remarked the Jesuit, quietly. "You think not!" cried her ladyship, somewhat astonished. "I hope you may be right; but I see no loophole anywhere. I had hoped that this debate would have helped us; but, instead of that, it seems as though the enemies of God are triumphant. Whatever we may think, it is generally accepted that the Protestants have won all along the line. Could you not, Father Ritzoom, answer him? You are skilled in all these matters." "It is a great mistake to think that these greag subjects can be dealt with on the public platform amidst clamour and excitement," replied the Jesuit. "The holy St. Paul tells us that spiritual things are spiritually discerned, it is not-arguments that will win converts, but grace. In one sense this. debate has been a colossal mistake; still I trust ~ may use it as a weapon which will vanquish tilt, enemies of the Church, and win numberless converts." "But how ? " cried Alizon.
"By converting Mr. Rutland," said Ritzoom, quietly. _ _ _

He lad seen that Father Sheen had been dis- creetly silent during his absence, and thus he was able to introduce'his plans in his own way. "Convert Mr. Rutland!" cried the girl. "Just that, Miss Alizon."

"Impossible." "Is the grace of God confined, Miss Alizon ? Is the power of the Church limited ? " said the priest, fixing his eyes steadily upon the girl. "Here is a great work for us all! By leading him into the fold, we save his own soul from Hell, and we save all those who will follow him. I can see in that young man a possible defender of faith; I can see him pleading for the very things he has condemned; I can see him in that very hall denying the things he has proclaimed, and telling his present congre- gation that their only hope is in our Holy Church." The Jesuit spoke in low, impressive tones, and the girl felt that he had cast a kind of spell upon her. For the moment she seemed to have no will but his. He seemed to possess a kind of mesmeric power._ _

- "If it could only be," she murmured. "It can, if you, Miss Alizon, and you, Lady Neville, will help," said the priest. •As far as our will is concerned," said her lady- ship, "of course, you can depend on it; still, I cannot quite see how it is to be done. He is a pronounced heretic, a militant heretic, and what is more, he is an educated man."

"He is an heretic, Lady Neville, because he has never really understood the Church. He has never seen it, therefore he doea not know it. He has been reared in an atynosphere—in which we are regarded as enemies to God. He has been fed upon Protestant history. Let him feel the lies of Pro- testantism; let him feel the truth of the Church.* "Yes, but how? Where ? " "Where? Here."

"Here!" cried her ladyship, in astonishment. "Yes, here. Let him see our religion where such as he should see it. Let him feel its power iu a relined, beautiful home; let him see it expressed in beautiful lives. Let him breathe the atmosphere which ever pervades this historic house, and all things will become new to him." "Do you really think so?" asked her ladyship, scarcely knowing what she was saying. "if the whole teaching of my life is not a failure, if thirty years of close observation, and thirty years of careful study of men and women be not the foolishness of fools, it will be so. When I read his speeches; I thought it possible, probable; but after seeing him, and hearing him to-night, I am sure. As I eaid, it has been my business to know men for thirty years. To you it has been no secret, Lady Neville, and thus I can speak plainly, although I have never been privileged to know you till yesterday. You know that I have had to deal with delicate questions, and have been led into the society of all classes of individuals. In order to serve the Church, I have been obliged to study men and motives closely. Well, I have had a special opportunity of understanding Rutland, for there is no place where a man's strength and weak- ness can be so clearly seen as on a public platform." For a long time they talked, each referring to the Jesuit in everything, and he, naturally, taking the place of teacher and adviser. To Lady Neville the plan seemed good, and holy, especially as it was advocated by a renowned priest of the Church. She felt it her duty to do her part, and she could see no objection to her falling in with all that was required of her. As for Alizan, she was fascinated by Father Ritzoom, and moved to admiration by his desire to win a heretic back to the truth. She did not dream of the results; she felt no pre- monition concerning the possible tragic outcome of what they were discussing. Neither did it enter her mind that she was regarded by the priest as the principal actor in the drama. Very well," said Lady Neville, as the priests left the Priory that night, "everything shall be arranged as you suggest."
CHAPTER XII. THE FIRST LINK IN THE CHAIN.
"Weal, aiv think things ev settled daan middlins, Mester Rutland."

It was old Matthy Bray who spoke to Duncan on the steps of Tudor Chapel. They had just come from one of the meetings of the church, and were on the point of going home. Several days had elapsed since the night when Duncan had given his lecture.
"After storm comes a calm," laughed the young minister.
"Aw doan't understand it, " remarked the weaver. "No, moor do aw," said Jonas Dixon, who, with two or three others, had come out with them. "Don't understand what.?" asked Rutland.
"Sheen and the Cathlicks bein' so quiet; it's noan like 'ern. Aw reckon they've suruntat else in their sleeves."
"What can they have? "

"Aw doan knt;W ; but ther's not one of 'em bin writin' to th' papers, and nobody's said a word. We all knaw as aa tha gived 'em a rare licken, but they'd a noan settled dean so quiet, ef they 'adn't bin tould to. Aw knew 'em too weel for that." "li," chimed in Jonas Dixon, "aw doan't forgeet thet Buggart Clough job. Why doan't ee tell all th' truth baat filet job, Mester Rutland?" "Because—well, there are good reasons."

aw spoase soa. But Ulcer, aw'm noan afeeard of a good ran. A dog as barks rarely isn't as ugly as th' one what 'nags 'is vend and growls; and it seems to me as an that's what Sheen's lot are doin'. What dost than think, Matthy ?" "Aw think thou'rt reight, Jonas. Weel, we mun kip aar een oppen, that's all. But mind, Mester Rutland, foaks of all sooarts are watchin' thee. Tha'st put thys_en on a 'igh plaace, and naa, church. bake, and -Cathlicks, as weel as all th' chapel foaks, 'll watch all tha dust. We look on thee as a sooart ov defender of th' faith, and if tha mak's ony slips, the very chaps as shasted praises bast tha, and said than wert champion,' 'll be the first to call thee nannies." "Yeq, I expect so." _

"Yi, Lancashire foals are the best in th' world, aw reckon, hut we ev ear faiiin's, we're noan but 'num. We're bit like th owd Jews. One day they shated : Hosanna! ' and th' next • Crucify Him! ' But theer, thoiCrt noan baan to mak' a fool o' tbysen, art a?" "I hope not." "Well then, my advice is this, and aw've noan. lived i' Lynford better ric,r fifty year for nowt_ Thee be careful if ony o' th' Cathiicks mak's friends wi' thee."
"Yes, rll be careful," laughed Duncan—but he had no fears.

"And theer's another thing. Thon'st kept away Ifro' the lasses rarely since thou'st bin here. If aw wur thee, aw'd geet wed." Dncan laughed heartily. "Pre never seen a imitable wife yet," he said. I "Well, that's thy fault. Ther's plenty o' nice lasses as belongs to Tudor, that thaa could 'ave for the min, and lasses wi' brass an all. Thor's Ashton's lasses, naa. Th' owd Ashton 'll gi"em ten thaasand apiece, awn towd, and Alice 'ud be a champion minister's wife. But theer, thet's noan aar business. 'Appen yo've got a lass somewhere." "No, I've not."

"Well, aw wish tha Wert wed. For.ks talk less abaat a passon when oo's wed." Matthy Bray and Duncan had by this time left the rest, and were walking in the direction of the young minister's lodgings. "Yu see, Mester Rutland," went on the old weaver, "we aal' oap thult stay at Tudor monv a
ar, and we Minx as ir ma had a good wiTa PO"' th' church, tha would Le a stake in till' ?ace, so ta spaik. And ther's nowt like .'avin' a stake in a place." "You think not
"It's th' great cure for moast things. Aw reckon if aw were s. rich man aw could kill most o' th' Socialism in a week." "Indeed."

"Yi, aw could Ef aw wer to give a cottage to every Socialist, hind stop his maath. Aw've seen it a lot o' times. It's chaps wot's got nowt who are Socialist. When they've got a bit o' brass, their Socialism goes.". _ _
"1 darei-ay ; but what has that to do with my getting a wife? ".

- "Ate, if thou'st gotton a wife fro' Lynford, thaa would'ave a stake 'ere. The roots o' thy bein' would be fastened 'ere. Besides, thy missis could go wi' thee to th' young fowk's meetin's, and thet ud stop gossip." "Why, have people been gossiping about me? " Ther's nobody been talked abaat as much, but riot i' that way. Aw'm only thinking baat the future. Thee look aat for a nice lass, mester. One with a bit o' brass, and thee settle daan at Tudor for life. But mind, oo mun come fro' Tudor."

"Must she ? " "Yi, oo must. Tudor foak 'ud noan put up wi' a lass from th' other chapels." "Good-night, -Matthy. I'm afraid you are a dangerous adviser," laughed Duncan. "Noa, aw'm on th' reight track. Aw've cut all my teeth, mester, an' aw'm wot th' lawyers ca' Icompus mentle. Aw reckon thet's it, but aw'm noan a Greek scholard, so 'appen tha'lt be laughin' at me."

"You are quite right," laughed Rutland. "Good- night," and he entered the door of his lodgings. On looking at his study table,, he found the following letter awaiting him: "The Priory, Lynford. "February 13th, 189—. "DEAR Ma. RUTLAND, —I have been much im- pressed by the fact that there is a good work which ought to be done in the town, and in which all the churches could take part. There are four cab- stand e in Lynford, besides those at the stations, and the only places of shelter which the cabmen have ara the nearest public-houses. This, for many reasons, is undesirable, especially as it has a tendency to lead men to be intemperate, who would Dtherwise be sober. I would, therefore, suggest that the representatives of all the principal churches should meet to consider the advisability of buildirig a sufficient number of convenient and comfortable cabmen's shelters. It is probable you may think the Priory a rather inconvenient place of meeting, nevertheless, I shall be very glad if you will come here on Friday night next (I understand that Friday is the night on which ministers are least engaged), so that we may, I trust, form some definite plan of action.—With kind regards, I am, yours sincerely,

"HELEN NEVILLE. " "N. B. —Time of meeting eight o'clock." Duncan read this letter through twice, and then laughed a little nervously'. "Of course, Father Sheen will be there," he thought, "but I can scarcely refuse. Tudor is the oldest and largest Nonconformist Church in the town, and ought to be represented. The object is a good one, too. I have often pitied those poor fellows standing around in the pouring rain. It will be awkward meeting Father Sheen and Lady Neville, but it is evident they bear no and I see no reason why I should be awkward. Yes, I'll go." He immediately scribbled a hasty acceptance of the invitaticn, and then went to the pillar-box which stood near his own door, and posted the letter.

"I wonder whether Miss Alizon Neville will be at the meeting?" he thought, as he came back to the house. "Scarcely, I should think. I have an idea that she will never speak to me again." When Friday night came he found his way to the Priory; he was rather late, owing to the fact that just,as he was about to start someone had called Asking him to visit a sick woman. It was therefore nearly half-past eight before he arrived at the house. Ire was immediately ushered into the room where a number of people sat, including Father Sheen.

Lady Neville's greeting as he entered was most cordial, and he could not help feeling that he was regarded as a person of importance in the meeting. On more than one occasion Father Sheen directly asked his opinion, and on his giving it, immediately advocated its acceptance. Indeed, the most friendly and genial person in the. room was the old priest. He told several funny stories with considerable spirit, and caused roars of laughter by them. For there is no part of the country where people are so easily moved to laughter as in Lancashire. Let a dozen men and women, of whatever degree, get together, and the poorest witticism will produce laughter, while a funny story will almost cause. convulsions. Lancashire people are what is generally termed "hard-headed,' they are as keen at driving a bargain as the proverbial Yorkshire- man, they will seldom err, on the side of generosity when business is concerned; nevertheless, they are simple-minded, tender-hearted people, as easily moved to laughter and tears as little children. And it is difficult to bestow higher praise than that in • a cynical and callous age. Presently the business of the meeting came to an end. Rutland's suggestion that a subscription list be opened, that her ladyship be the treasurer, and the town clerk the secretary, was passed without a dissentient, and a working committee was elected on the spot. Immediately this was done Father Sheen called Rutland aside and asked 'him a question on a matter which seemed to the young minister of but little importance, but which apparently exercised the old priest's mind greatly. Indeed, so interested did he become concerning the matter, and so earnestly did he talk, that Rutland, for courtesy's sake, was obliged to listen, and consequently a few minutes later he found that the rest of the members had departed, and that he was alone in the room with the old Irishman.

At this juncture Lady Neville entered the room. "I am so glad you are not gone, Mr. Rutland," she said, graciously. "I was anxious that you should not slip out without my having a chance of speaking to you. Alizon was telling me the other day that you were very fond of old houses. I thought you might like to look over the Priory." "1 should be delighted," replied Rutland, almost without thinking. "It is rather a fine old house in its way, I suppose," went on her ladyship, "and has many interestinc, associations. There are secret passages, secret cell's, places where traitors have been hidden, and outlaws sheltered. There is a haunted room, where the ghost of Sir Thomas More is supposed to appear, and a royal chamber where Charles I. is said to have slept. I shall be delighted to shew you through." "You are very kind," said Duncan. "I am afraid you have fastened upon a weakness of mine. I am simply a child when I am brought into con- tact with things old and mysterious. Thit I am afraid I am taxing your ladyship's kindness far too much by accepting." • .
"Oh no, .do not niention it. It will be a real pleasure to show you through the building. But what time is it, Father Sheen?"

"It is half-past nine," replied the priest. "Oh, I remember now. We dined very early to-night in view of this meeting, Mr. Rutland, and all this talking is exhausting. lam sure, Father Sheen, you will be glad of some slight refreshment, and I hope Mr. Rutland will consent to join us at a little supper. He will need it to fortify him- self against the ghosts," and her ladyship laughed pleasantly. Before he realised what he was doing he found himself in another room speaking to Alizon Neville. The young minister felt his heart beat faster as she held out her hand, and greeted him with a kind smile. Everything was so different from what he had expected. Instead of being cold and haughty, she was kind and gracious. He could tact help feeling how beautiful she was. There in the glow of the lamplight her finely-moulded form revealed itself to advantage, while her somewhat heightened colour, and bright, shining eyes were the accompaniment of a face, which to the young man was lovely beyond words. The great masses of wavy chestnut hair, which glistened in the light, seemed to the romantic young minister almost like a nimbus, and at that moment he forgot that he was a commoner, while she belonged to one of the oldest families in England, forgot that he was a Protestant, and that she was an ardent Catholic.

In spite of t-.1-le Socialistic tendencies of the age, England is a conservative country, and there is much truth in the old saying that an Englishman loves a lord. He does, and always will, I suspect, while we are a nation and remember that we have a history. Not that Rutland was a worshipper of aristocracy. Far from it. He was too sensible a fellow for that. And yet he was influenced by be fact that Alizon Neville came of a race which '3ad influenced the life of the country. Although ae did net know it, those old rooms, the Quaint

antique turniture, and the tact that the Yriory was associated with some of the important epochs of the English race, had a strange effect upon him. They talked about books, pictures, plays, ana men, and the time sped by on the wings of the wind. When they rose from the table, Pathter Sheen looked at his watch. "it is nearly half-past ten, Lady Neville," h. eft! stud, with mock seriousness. "Is it," cried Rutland, "I had forgotten—tits* is I had no idea it was so late. lam afraid I dare not tax you to take me over the Priory to-nigliat::„ "It is rather late," said Lady Neville. would take at least two hours. You must CO some other day, Mr. Rutland, come early. Caul you decide upon an afternoon now. Almost all day next week, I shall be delighted to see you. Rutland was fascinated, bewildered. Scarcell realising what he was doing he mentioned a day 031 which he would be at liberty. "That will be delightful," said Lady Neville, graciously. "You and Father Sheen will be able to g 6 back to Lynford together; but there is plentl, of time for you to smoke a cigar before leaving us. She led the way into the library, and the two, men smoked and talked, while Lady Neville Alizon joined in their conversation. Rutland ft"; that this was the most delightful evening he hay' ever spent. "Next Wednesday, then, at three o'clock, I shill! expect you both," said her ladyship. "You will then be able to go over the house before dinner quite comfortably. Good-night." The two men walked towards Lynford, while Lady Neville went back to Alizon. "He is really a delightful young fellow to know, she remarked, as Alizon sat looking into the fire. "Yes," replied the girl. "I had no idea he would be so interesting. is really worth knowing apart from every other consideration." "Do you think all this is quite right, mother? asked the girl. "I do, indeed. We are simply kind to him,an3 —that is all. If we succeed, he will thank li throughout his life. Besides, it is our duty." , "Do you think he will ever become a convert? "Yes, I think so, don't you? " "No," replied Alizon, "I do not believe, he will ever be a Catholic."
"I believe on are mistaken," replied Lad! Neville. "Yon will see that lam right in a fes° **leeks."
(To be continued.)
RESTLESS CHILDREN.

A Misfortune more than a Fault. At this time of the year all children suff -r more or less from the heat ; eve" the tsest of them become rest- - less and d fficult to manage, but in high-Tirited eXCit ahle children the condition sometimes develoPs oa° alarming di-gve. Parents will do well to watch for Mil first &ens of nervous excitement and profit by' !Eason taught to one father in Monmouthshire to great cost. Last year a continual restlEs4ness nbcerved in his second son, a. boy of seven, but ttoi°r" naturally a high-spiritel lad, little notice was taken. Last July, however, this condition became so Prir nounced that he was really only quiet when aslee9'. Frequently his limbs were powerless, and he had to fed by others.. Medical aid was called in, and the oat was doscribld as a severe form of St. Vitu6' datict; removal to s. hrspital was recommended, but as parents were informed he would have to spend fra':, eigt.teen 'months to three years there, this advicf! not acted upon. In August the boy was tale : n awaV tt-,e hope that a change might prove beneficial, hut 131 this time the right side and arm wore paralysed, a° then paralysis extended to the left side. Matters went from had to worse, according, to a statement snails ta a " South Wales Ciaz-itte " leportlti who saw the child. The father explained: "A fe,,5 &ye later he was seized with a lit of yawning : rtec-a morning he awoke in pain and completely helples6 a : speechless. For rive weeks he suffered the inost-eXoL° elating agony, and his 'tries were heartrending. Puvt was redezed to a mere skeleton, and was a pitiful !OP' indeed ! A AO "All hope of saving the child was abandoned, 5m...., decided to bring him home. I had to carry him in arms like the merest infant. div.head: " BRAWLING " IN A WARRINGTON
div.p: " BRAWLING " IN A WARRINGTON
CHAPEL.
Disgraceful Scene. A Lot of Hypocrites."

William Charles Hastings, 5, Percy-street.was brought Up at the Warrington Police Court on Monday, on a Charge of being guilty of violent behaviour in the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist Chapel,Crosfield-street at 3 o'clock on Sunday afternoon.—He pleaded guilty. Mr. F. R. Roberts who prosecuted on behalf of the Chapel authorities said that the offance was fortunately as rare as it was serious and after the plea of the Prisoner puha!), be need not say very much about it. From tine to time past the prisoner had entertained a most i..sane jealousy of his wife. Unfortunately he had been drinking and that no doubt, was the explanation of the whole matter. His wife was a woman of excellent Character and a regular attender at the Welsh Chapel, and in every way had done ner best to set her husband a better example. Instead of following the example.the man had allowed himself to entertain this insane jealousy and it culminated a month ago in his leaving ihis wife and going to America. A fee days ago he returned and ey -r since he had pursued his wife with Considerable bitterness and malice. While the congrega- tion arid Sunday school scholars were at worship in the Welsh Chapel at a quarter to three on Sunday af•ernoon the prisoner broke through the door in a very noisy way and in a loud voice, and in the hearing of the whole of the congregation, and in fact to their alarm, he began to make a very shocking and serious charge against hi. wife. The authorities, of c airse,were dumbfounded for a time but when they had recovered their senses one or two of them went to the prisoner and began to reason 'With him. Prisoner had a stick in his hand and his malice and antipathy was turned for the moment from his wife to the gentlemen who remonstrated with him. tie said they were "a lot of hypocrites " and that the chapel was a-- canting place and when one of the 'ACers reasoned with him he took off his coat and %tteninted to strike him with the stick. This was going for some minutes and the effect nas such that Mrs. castings fainted and had to be carried out, and scores children in alarm rushed out of the huildin4 and „ Ittediately the entire congregation was broken up. A ;1113°I'e shocking case of brawling he had never read or Card of in his life ; for the man to go to the chapel and 1:10t only make a horrible charge agains: his wife in a Place of worship in the presence of GA, and to follow it up by accusins Christians of hyocrisy and threaten- erg to strike oni of the offt,sre with his stick. Imme- diately he was got out of the building be proreeded to renew the disturbance outside. One of the officers who had been despatched for a constable arrived and the man was taken in charge. - - _

Emmanuel Jones, ouo of the church officers save evidenco. Prisoner expressed his sorrow for what had occurre& fle had had some drink and he went to chapel to see it big children were there and not with the intention of creating a disturbance. He could not s-e his children and ttia enraged him. It was the drink that caused it all.

The Chairman (Mr Birchall) said it was a very serious ()Nine and the puhlic must understand that a Christian congregation most hive the right to worship in peace. Prisoner would he fined 20i and costs with the alternative Of a munth's imprisonment.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT PRESTON BROOK Prisoner Committed.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT PRESTON BROOK Prisoner Committed.

Alfred Wright., described as a fansmith, of Haverton Hill, near hfiddleshurgh, crag on Wednesday brought before the Runcorn Bench, charged with attempting suicide at Preston Brook, on Friday last, by cutting his throat and aftqrwards jumping into the Bridgewater Canal. The following evidence %vat taken : Estha Ann Jones, married woman. residing at Preston-o'th'•Hill, on Friday last about 3 o'clock, saw the man sitting nn the stable wall opposite the house in which sh, lived, and which was on the canal bank. She afterwards saw him leaning over the wall for some time and when he came away, she noticed that his hands vrere covered wirla blood, and that he staggered very tnuch.

Josenh Prie4tly. contractor, of Preston-o'th'-Flill, stid about 3.30 on Friday last he was standing on the canal bank, and noticed the prisoner coming towards the eridgewater Canal. His hands were covered with blond, and he was bleeding from the throat. Witness saw the raan jump into the canal bead first from the opposite aide to that on which he was standing. Prisoner came to the surfaee and swam across to the side witness WAS atanding. Prison.r did not say anythine, neither did witness ; but he me ieed that pri +otter had the knife (Produced) in his right hand. Then witness said to him "put that knife away," but prisoner made no reply, nor did he put the knife away. Prisoner, who was then near to the side of the canal, stool upright in the canal for a few minutes but afterwards jumped towards the middle again. Wit- ness then shonted to some boat peonle on the other side to throw a boat hook, and they did so. Another man, John Clare, got t'ne boa'. hook Anil nulled the prisoner to the side with it. Witness assisted in getting the man out. There was no trouble in getting prisoner out as he did not resist, hut he did seem to be nearly eatmusted by that time. He did not speak and wa4 subs, qeently taken to the W•ekhonse. Witness did net know the Prisoner wh was lint a native of Preston-e'th'-Hill

John Clare, carpenter and storekeeper at Pres"on Brook, stated in cot s-quence of an alarm be wenr to the canal eide at abent 3.20 on Friday. Re 81w the prisoner in the canal aa s'at'd by the previous wanes% with a hnife in hi a hand Ey, akin saw blood upon the man's 'whiskers and front. He assisted in getting him ow. John Hidoewac. constable at Prestnn n'tl-.' Hill. bout 5 30 on FrAIS he went to Dutton Workh luae and tound prisoner .rith a had wound in his thrnat in 'he hospital ward ot the insti'ution. On the following Tuesdar he 'ain went to the WorkhnuFe and arreated Prisoner wh)m chargod with att,.ropting to commit

suicide by cutting his throat and then jumping into th canal. The man replied "I am as sunsible as you ar now but then I didn't know what I was doing." Thomas James Selby surgeon practising at Frodsham and nr dical officer to the Runcorn Union Workhouse, at Dutton, said he was at the Workhouse about 5 o clock on Friday afternoon wirn tbe prisoner was brought in. Be examined the man and found him to be suffering from a large wound in the front of his throat right over the larynx ;it was wry irregular and about 2-!2- inches long. The wound he would say was likely to be inflicted by a knife similar to that p:oduced. No important blood vessels had been divided. The knife had came in contact with the clrti'age of the larynx stopping its further progress. Prisoner's clothing was wet through, and be would not give any account of himself,though he seemed to know what was going on. . . .
-: The Bench eommitted prignner to the next Assizes to be held at linutsford on the 15th of October next. Bail was ;Allowed in sureties of £lO personal, and two ethers of £5.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL COMPANY. Official Changes.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL COMPANY. Official Changes.

The Board of Directors of the Ship Canal Company Limited, regret to havo to state that continual indis- position has led Mr. W. H. Collier to resign his position of Manager of the Ship Canal and Bridgewater Depart- ments. Mr. John C. vVilleon has also retired from the active position of Assistant Manager, Imause he wished to be relieved from the responsibility of the position and have lighter duties. He will, however, continue to take charge of some important Ship Canal Traffic matters. Tire undermentioned new appeintments have been made::—Mr Ernest Latimer, formerly accountant to te general sanerintendent ; Mr Herbert M Gibson,formerly chief traffic agent, to be chief traffic superintendent.; with charge of Ship Cadal traffic negotiations; Mr F A Eyre, formerly assistant accountant, to be accountant Mr John Oldfield retains his position of Superintendent Bridgewater Department.

Purgatives, tonics, headache powders, cannot cure you. Death of the Rev. G. Allton.

The parisnioners of 6t. BArnabas'. Warrington,re • ceived the news last week end of the death of the Rev. George Allton, which occurred at bia residence at. Bridgford, Nottingham, at 10.30 on Friday morn- ing. The deceased, who had been in a delicate state of health for some time, was vicar of St. Baruabas' Church] for thirteen years. Ile resigned the living last year, Before commencing his sermon on Sun- day evening,the Vicar (Rev. J. G. Hollingworth) alluded to the event and expressed sympatey with the bereaved relatives. The funeral took place on Monday, a beautiful wreath being forwarded by the parishioners. Resignation of the Rev. W. H. Drummond. itev IV H Drummond has sent in his resigna- tion as pastor ot the, Unitarian Chapel, Cairo-street, which position he has hel,l for the past seven years having accepted the charge of All Souls, Belfast. The resignation was accepted on Sunday morning with much regret by the congregation, and it is ex• pected that Mr. Drummond will leave Warrington for his new sphere of labour some time during the month of September. His departure from Warring- ton will create a vacancy on the Boar • of Guardians, with which he has been identified for several years. He has always taken considerable interest in Poor Law work, and was rarely absent from either the fort ni4ht ly meetings of the Board of Guardians or the meerings of till, commit- tees of which he will a member,
