div.head: TEE E\ A NIINEti, FRIDAY, JULY 20, 1900.
div.p: TEE E\ A NIINEti, FRIDAY, JULY 20, 1900.
c..) sit with you a little," closed the door again aria left Katherine with the sick woman.

She approached cautiously to the becis;ae, 'pito knowing what sort of reception she miel t expect; but the sight which met her eyes struck her dumb with astonishment. Mrs. Thompson had mentioned Miss Nelson as a young woman, but had given no hint of her uncommon personal beauty. What Mrs. Temple saw was the figure of a girl, not over twenty, who lay back in the bed white as death, and almost as unconscious.

Her golden hair, unbound, lay in long straiths ever the pillow. Her large eyes, half-closed, had DO life in them. Her lips were blue, her mouth open; she had every appearance of a dying creature. AR,Tleril2 bent over the bed and hastily: "Miss Nelson! Miss NetiZOiii- Try anct rouse yourself! What made you do this thing, my dear? What made you try to take your life? Don't you know that it is a sin, a crime, and that you have no right to shorten an existence which has but just begun ? " The girl looked so much as if she were sinking into the sleep of Death that Katherine thought the best way of rousing her: would be to startle and, perhaps, frighten her 'a little, by this boldness on the part of a stranger, in immediately addressing her on the subject of her private affairs. And it had the desired effect. The girl slightly opened her eyes and said: "Who are you?"

"Only a woman like yourself, who has known deep trouble, but who has never been tempted to take her life in consequence!" "You can never have known such trouble as mine," said the stranger, and then, rousing herself a little, she continued fretfully: "Ohl why did they fuss over me like that and send for a doctor? What's the good? I shall only have the trouble of doing it all over again." Uric, VQ: You not do that, I am sure," said Katherine "aines y. "You are young • you hare all your life before you; there may be a bright future ahead. Don't give way to despair. However hard your' trouble may be to bear; there is always a way out of it." "That shews how. Much you know Abut it!" replied the girl. "There is no way 6Wt of my trouble but death. If you knew who Ad what I am, you would shrink from me to the fuattest end of the room."

At these words Katherine did Sbrink it little. Virtuous women are so unused to come iti contact with their fallen sisters that the first experience is apt to prove rather startling. But. she conquered her natural feelinf of aversion, and laid her hand upon Miss Nelson s instead. "You must not say that," she answered gently; "we have all sinned, you know, in one way and another, and God makes no distinction between us. It is He only Who can determine the greatness or smallness of our sin. Trust in Him, my dear, and He will bring you through these deep waters, and set your feet in a dry place." "You don't know what you're talking about," replied the sick girl. At that moment a fearful spasm of pain passed over her face, and her features twitched with agony. "Are you in pain again ? " asked Katherine anxiously. "Yes, was the reply, "awful pain. They didn't get all the poison out of me, and I'm glad of it. I want to die. Where's the use of living? I shall never see him again!" "Let me send for the doctor," cried Katherine, flying to the bell. "Stop!" cried the dying girl; "there's someone elle I want to see that would do me more good than all the doctors fat the world! I'm dying, I tell you. What's the good of troubling the doctor ? " "Who is it you want to see ? " demanded Katherine.
"The man I care for—the man I love," replied Carrie Nelson. "I've ruined his life, but he'll forgive me for it when he sees me die! I've done it all for him—all for him!" •

"But why—why?" asked her companion, curious to learn the particulars of the girl's history. "I eared for him so, he was pleasant and hand- some, and I got him away from his home; but it was all of no use. He couldn't forget his own friends; and he was always grieving after what he had lost, till he took to abusing me for having been the means of his losing it. And then I saw he had tired of me, and I taxed him with it, and lie said it was true, so I just left him one morning and came here. I hoped a little that he would be sorry then, and come after me; but, when I found he didn't, I resolved to end it altogether. And I've done it. Ah " concluded the girl with a long groan. "You must let me send for the doctor! "exclaimed Katherine.

"No, no! Send for him instead. I shan't last long enough to say all I have to say now. But if I don't, tell him from me to go back to his wife and ask her to forgive him—she will if she loves him as he says she did—and let him be happy—be happy once again. Ah I" with another moan. "A married man!" said Katherine, thinking of her own wrong. "Oh! how could you have taken him from his wife? Do you know what women suffer when they are deceived by the man they trust in?"

"And do you know what the men suffer when they have deceived them ? " said the girl with a temporary animation. "If you had heard will moan and cry after his wife, you would! He began a few days after we had been together, and he never left off till we parted. He used to say she was the best and purest. and most loving woman in the world, till I was sick of hearing her praises. And it was all my fault that he left her! I had got spooney on him, and I saw that he admired me, so I laid a trap for him one day, and he was too much ashamed to go home afterwards. But I must see him—l _must see him before I die, to hear him say that he forgives it all! Oh! send for him, do send for him; I can't die else!"
"Of course I will send for him, if you will tell nae,his name, and where to send," said Katherine.
"Captain Wilfrid Temple, 102, Cornwall-terrace, Regent's Park," replied Carrie Nelson faintly.

Katherine started. It came as a blow to her to find she had been solacing the last hours of the woman who had been the cause of all her bitter trouble. And to be entrusted, too, to bring her husband to her bedside! At first she thought she could not do it. She felt more like denouncing the poor creature before her, and telling her to die without the unhallowed consolation for which she craved. But Katherine Temple was a good woman. She had tried through life to do what she should, rather than what she desired; so she restrained her tongue, and saying quietly: "I will send a wire to him at once, left the room to summon both the doctor and Captain Temple to Carrie Nelson's deathbed.

The messages "despatched, she went to her own 'room for a moment to collect her scattered thoughts. So this was the girl for whom her Wilfrid had deserted her! She was very lovely—Katherine's jealousy even could not deny that—and yet she had not. had the power to keep him. He had moaned and cried after his wife—so she had declared—after the lapse only of a few weeks of unlicensed pleasure. He could not forget, even in the midst of it all, now much she had loved and cared for him, and believed in him, as she believed in herself. At first her indignation got the better of her charity. "Let him moan and cry! "she said. "I am glad to hear it. I have cried enough over him, God knows! Let him feel something of the agony of loss that I have gone through!" But in a little while better thoughts came to her. Was she the one to judge him? Did she even understand his nature sufficiently to be able to appraise the extent of the temptation which had come to him? Could any woman judge a man fairly in such circumstances, she, whom the Creator had endowed ,with so much calmer and repressible a temperament? And then the words came into her mind: "Forgive us our trespases. as we forgive them that trespass against us." ,-Had she actually been repeating that Divine prayer morning and evening for the last twelve mouths without applying it to the husband whom she had adored, whom she adored still? Katherine was feel ng very self-condemnatory and humiliated when her train of thought was interrupted by a knock upon her bedroom door and the voice of Mr.. Thompoon entreating her to go back to the side of Mipg
ilhvo you sent off that telegram ?" inquired Katherine Temple. .as she confronted the landlady.

Yeti, madam, sotne time ago; but the poor lady seems getting. much worse, and really I feel afraid to stay alone with her. Her face has turned finite grey, and there's a kind of froth every now ..:od then upon her lips. Do, please, come and wait with me till Dr. Graham arrives!"

"Certainly, if r, be of any use," said Mrs. Tonio!e wearily; "but Miss Nelson has sent, for a gentleman friend, and when he conies you must let me go, as I do not wish to see him." "Ah! I don't expect as the poor young creature will live long enough to see any of her friends again," replied Mrs. Thompson. "It's my belief that she's going as fast as she can. Oh! thank goodness, here's the doctor." And, accompanied by the medical man, who had hatmened to be at home when the messeatter went

for hini, they proceedect to Carrie Aelson's room. She was evidently dying: the most unpractised observer could have seen as much. Her eyes were glazing, and her hands incessantly plucked at the counterpane that covered her. "Has she any friends whom she might wish to see again 7" demanded the doctor, as they stood in silence round her bed. _ _

_ "She has wired for one, I hear," replied the landlady. "Well, the sooner they come the better. She is sinking fast," was the reply. "It is of no use my remaining here, Mrs. Thompson. I can do nothing more for her. You can let me know when it is all over. and I will sign the certificate; but I am afraid you will not be able to avoid an inquest." "Then she must go to a mortuary, for I won't have it in my house," expostulated Mrs. Thompson. "Hush!" interposed Katherine; "she opened her eyes.' - "Has he come ? " articulated, with difficulty, the dying girl. "He will be here in a minute," said Katherine, soothingly, and, indeed, at that moment a cab stopped outside the house, and a double knock resounded on the hall-door. "Here he is," she cried breathlessly, as she tried to make her escape. "All—all—go!" said Carrie Nelson faintly. The doctor and landlady stepped outside the room, to encounter a handsome, stalwart man of about thirty, who came up the stairs with a troubled countenance. Dr. Graham explained the state of affairs to him, and accompanied him back into the room, whilst Katherine flew into the drawing-room, which was divided from that of the dying woman by folding doge, _gow he,r I/4Z belt! To be so near him—he, wh-6-ii'as all the world to her—and yet to be unable to acknowledge her presence, or to speak one word to him! She heard the murmur of voices in the next room, an tlxm (;:octos Wt, and followed Mrs. ThOTUTTI dnitiriairs; They two—Wilfrid Temes and Carrie Salsoa---who had so wronged heT, who had broken her heafi, repo left together and alone. How Katherine longed 13 htais NA. voice once more, the voice she had so loved, which had been silent for her for twelve lorig months! The folding doors between the rooms were not quite closed, and she advanced as close as she could towards them; for she did not think it was dishonourable to listen to what her husband might say, for, whatever it might be, she cared for hint still too much ever to betray him, or to cast any reproaches in his teeth. So she. stopped there, hardly daring to breathe, lest Wilfrid should dis- cover and Wrens her. _ _

"Carrie! he commenced, "it grieves me beyond measure to find you like this. Whatever made you do so rash an act? You knew that 1 would always provide for you." "But you could not /at me," was the answer, slowly and painfully given. "Don't. re-open that vexed question at such a moment," replied Captain Temple; "men cannot effect impossibilities. But whatever you did, poor girl, you did for love of me, and if you spoilt my life lam not the one to reproach you. Forget it all now. Think only of where you are going. "I—cannot—forget---it," gasped the dying girl. "I wane yui to promise me two things—that you will forgive Me, and ask your wife to forgive us both."

"I can promise the first readily, Carrie. I for- give you from the bottom of my heart. You sinned for my sake, and I was a coward to let you sacrifice yourself. But the other is impossible. My wife is a good, pure woman, and would never overlook or forgive a sin like mine. Don't speak of it any more." "But where is she ? " cried Carrie, trying to raise herself in bed. "Fetch her to me, and I will tell her all—how I met you at the theatre, and fell in love with you, and followed you to your rooms, and that it was all my fault—only mine—and that you never wanted me and never loved me! " "I cannot fetch her to you. I don't know where she is," said Wilfrid Temple with a sigh, "but better than with me, at any rate. Lie down again, Carrie, and be at peace. Whatever I may suffer I fully deserve." "Oh if she knew all—how good you are—how you lamented over the ruin I brought upon you— how you love her still, she could not help heiself ; she must forgive you!" "Yes, yes," he answered soothißgly, "it will all be right some day; don't worry yourself about it now. Forgive me, Carrie, if I caused you pain; but, once convinced of the great sin of which I had been guilty towards God and my wife, I could not keep you longer near me—it had become impossible —but I little dreamt it would end in this!"

"Forgive vie," ejaculated the dying girl, "and kiss me once more, Will only once more. She would not mind, if she knew that I—l—was— dying." Katherine could not hear, but she could imagine that the lips of these two, so soon to be parted for ever, had met again, for a short silence was succeeded by a heavy sigh, and then a startled exclamation in her husband's voice. She guessed the truth. Poor Carrie Nelson had gone to her last account. Katherine drew back hastily from her place of hiding, as Captain Temple's footsteps were beard advancing to the door, presumably to call for assistance. But, to her dismay, instead of summoning Mrs. Thompson or the doctor, he turned the handle of the drawing-room door, and in another moment he stood before her.

"My God! Katherine'" he exclaimed, "where on earth have you sprung from ? " "I am staying in this house," she replied in a trembling voice, "and I have been attending on Miss Nelson during the morning." "You—nursed—her?! he said. "And did you know who she was ? "

"Not till I sent the wire for you." "You sent that wire ? " "I did. Why not? Could I refuse to gratify a dying woman's last wish?" "And you have been here all the time? You have heard what passed between us?" "Every word. I hope you will not think I was wrong to listen. I thought I had a right to hear." "I am glad you did. You know now, at all events, that, however wickedly and dishonourably I have behaved to you, I have not been so lase as to forget the love of which I was unworthy." "I see you did not." _ _

"And now I will not stay a moment to defile your presence by my own. Let me thank you, Katherine, for the love which shed a sunshine over my life for so many happy years, and ask you, if you cannot think of me without pain, sometimes to pray that we may yet meet. in a world where I may be purified from all that makes you hate me now."

"I have never hated you, Wilfrid. Perhaps I have judged you too harshly. We women know so little of the temptations which assail a man, and sometimes make him forget everythin; except_ his own carnal nature and the gratification of a moment. Our ignorance tnakes us appear too harsh sometimes and too unforgiving. But that poor girl somewhat opened my eyes, in showing me that a man may fall outwardly, and yet retain the best feelings of his manhood—his respect for purity, and love, and fidelity. So I forgive you freely. Let poor Carrie's self-inflicted death be the mediator between us, to bring us kinder and more pitiful feelings for each other in the future. We loved each other once--"

"God knows we did! God knows I love you still; if possible, better than before, and certainly with a holier, worthier love than I felt when I wronged you. Katherine, when I see how your pure love can induce you to palliate the fault of one so utterly unworthy of forgiveness as myself -" he said in a broken voice. "We. have all sinned and come short of His glory," she answered softly. "Yes; and in another world, perhaps --" he whispered..
"And why not in this world, Wilfrid? It was for this world that we were created, to help each other on the road to a better."

"But can you—is it possible? "he asked wistfully. "I have;" she answered. "Wilfrid, we are one. Did not God join us? Then who shall separate us?" "Katherine! my wife!" he exclaimed joyfully, as he opened his arms, "am I really forgiven?" "Yes, dearest, even as we trust that God will forgive us both," she replied, as she nestled her head upon his shoulder. "0 Wilfrid, home at last! My home, which I thought I should never see again. Dearest, let us forget all the past! Let it be laid with that poor child in her grave! I know now that, you were more sinned against than sinning, and Heaven knows it too. But you and I—let no man put us asunder." f'Never--never again! So help me God," he replied, as they stood there silent with their great soy, and hearing nothing but the beating of each other's hearts.

div.p: (Copyright.) A DIVINE FORGIVENESS.
BY. FLORENCE MARRYAT,
Author of "Love's Conflict," "My ONVII Child," "My Sister the Actress," "Her Lord and Master," "The face in the conservatory.
"To err is human; to forgive, ciivinr."

Is there anything in this world more detestable than a London fog? It oppresFes the health and spirits even of the young and the gay. it. drives the sorrowful and the pessimistic to despair. To watch the thick, yellow mist creep into the room until it envelops all surrounding objects. making the gas burn dim, and everything you touch feel damp and clammy; to look from the blurred window-panes upon a sheet of mystery, through Which occasionally the faint light from a passing tab'or-a link-boy glimmers; and then to turn back with a heavy sigh to the interior of your sitting- room, where even a large fire cannot prevent the encroaching fog from stinging your nostrils and making your eyes water

Katherine Temple felt it more than she had been used to do as shortly after her return to England she sat crouched in an arm-chair before the fire in the apartments she temporarily occupied. She had crossed from Nice but a few days previously, and taken the rooms chosen for her by her mother, Mrs. Franklyn, till some business connected with her property was settled. But she already wished that she ha-i not come. The wretched, dismal day, the strange rooms and furniture, and the time— just a year since her great inifortune—all com- bined to make her feel suicidal.

Mrs. Franklyn had wished her to go to her house—she wished Katherine to do so many things tlit were not in accordance with her inclinations Mrs. Temp!e d:,:ided that she would ratllier be alone. rt wi sizificieTitly painful to her to. revisit England just at that period, without being compelled to listen to animadversions on her husband's conduct and her own wrongs. The dim light made her throw down the newspaper impatiently, and draw as close to the fire as she could; and as she remained staring into the blazing coals the circumstances of her life passed in review before her.

She felt very lonely. She had not a friend near her at that moment. She had no children to occupy her attention, no husband's wishes to consult; not even a cat to rub its soft fur against her dress and purr its content into her ear, or a faithful dog to thrust its wet, cold nose into her hand and assure her of its unspoken sympathy. But last year, only twelve months ago, how different all things had been with her. Then she had had a husband whom she thoroughly believed to be true and faithful—a husband whom she adored, in whom her whole life had been wrapped up; and, occupied with him, a pleasant home in which, surrounded by every comfort, she had fully enjoyed the love and luxury which she had expected 0 enjoy to the end. And then had fallen the blow which had seemed to finish everything at once—the greatest trouble that can befall a loving woman, that crushed her to the earth, making her, at first, too indignant for words, and then too despairing to argue or reply ; her husband, her Wilfrid, whom she loved so dearly, had deceived her, left her for another woman, committed the unpardon- abl sin in mntrimony—had been unfaithful. Her mother and her friends had gathered about her at that period and entreated her to go to law with him, to procure a legal separation, and rid herself of the wretch for ever. But something in Katherine's nature shrank from the idea; some- thing made it impossible to her. How could she cast away the man she had sworn to love and honour, as if he had been an article of worn-out clothing; separate herself for ever from the being who had shared her bed and board and been her constant companion? Other wives might find it feasible even to console themselves in such circum- stances, but to Katherine Temple it was impossible. She could not even argue the matter. She knew' it was true, and that was enough for her. So she had crept away from Captain Temple's house as if she had been the culprit instead of him, and, having a small income of her own, had passed her time since in wandering about foreign places, very lonely and very miserable, but anxious before everything to avoid the condolence of her friends, which hurt her more than all else could do. And so she found herself once more in London, though bereft of all she held dear on earth, and painfully reminded of the the fact by her surroundings. _ _

She did not know where her husband might be at that moment. She did not even know the name of the woman for whom he had deserted her. She had been made aware of the fact by his own con- fession, and that had been enough for her, enough to break her heart (so she told herself) ; and apres vale Deluge. She was musing after this fashion, wishing the fog would clear away, wondering if she could get a cab to take her anywhere from herself, when she was startled by her landlady bursting into the room without ceremony, and, after throwing herself into a chair, dissolving into tears and rocking to and fro. "Good gracious! Mrs. Thompson! " exclaimed Katherine, "whatever is the matter ? "

"Matter, Mrs. Temple!" was the reply. "Matter enough, I can assure you! Such a thing never happened in my house before, and I have been a householder now for twenty years. It's a di,,-rrace! an infamy! and it will ruin my business!" " int what is it ? What are you alluding to ? " aske I her lodger, glad of any diversion from her sad thoughts. "The lady upstairs!" gasped Mrs. Thompson, "in the back drawing-room ! She's tried to commit suicide! Taken poison! and the doctor says it'• ten to one if she'll get over it! _ . _

"How shocking!'" cried Katherine, her sympa- thies roused at once. "But why did the poor thing"do it? Was it an accident ? " "That I can't tell you," was the reply. "All I know is that, hearing a groaning in her room about an hour ago, I went in to see if she was ill, and found her stretched on the floor and lavender- .lour in the face. I sent for Dr. Graham, who lives down the street, at once, and he had to use the stomach-pump, but says that he is not at all sure that she will get over it, as she won't speak, and he doesn't know how long before it MS that she had swallowed the stuff. And fancy. a death by poison and a funeral in my house! Why, the whole neighbourhood will get scent of the story, and we shall never hear the last of it."

"But who is nursing the lady ? And what is her name? Has she any friends with her? "She called herself Miss Nelson to me, but I'm sure I don't know if that's her real name or not. People who come to a respectable house to take poison may not choose to give their real names. But she's been here over a week now, and she seemed very quiet and paid regular, so who could have ..thought--" _ _ _
"Yes, -yes," interposed Katherine Temple, anxious to check the landlady's garrulity, "but is Miss Nelson alone? Is no one with 11,-r ?"

"Who should be with her ? " replied the woman sharply. "I have no time to watch beside suicides. nor my servants either, and if the doctor thinks • it necessary he must send in a hospital nurse—that is. if she has the money to pay for one. I only hope the funeral expenses won't come upon me." "Dui, meanwhile, she may attempt her life again, and with better success." said Katherine. "I am sure she ought to be watched, if only for humanity's sake, Mrs. Thompson." "Perhaps so, madam, but I have the other lodgers' dinners to see after: and I really don't know if toy servant would condescend to sit beside a young \roman that has attempted murder! She might take a fancy to try it on someone else nest. Oh, I would give everything I possess not to have had it happen in my house!" 'lt's too late to think of that now,' 55;d Katherine, "and if you reslly have no one who can watch Miss Nelson for a little while, / will do so, Mrs. Thompson." "Int.! yos, madam?" exclaimed this landlady. "Why not? I ant sure there is little enouch do this dreadful day, and 1 shall be quite thank- ful for some wholesome work. Tell me what Di% ctraham's orders were, and 1 will go up to the sick room at once."

"Well, I'm sure it's uncommonly good of you." said Mrs. Thompson, able to recog,nise tha beauty of an ac!ion which she could not enin. • ;:n : its taking a lot of trouble for a stranger : hut the doctor said she was to-be waathed till his reiurn, and to take small doses of brandy and wal.er every half-hour or so, and he would come aga'n in the ereni.ng.".

"That, is easy enough." replied Katherine. "And now, if you will shew me the way, I will go up to the poor creature at once." The landlady thereupon led the way upstairs to the back drawing-room, which was furnished as a bedroom, and having said: "I hope you are feeling better, mules; here's a lads as will be rood enough

It was decided that the Clerk should write and inform the sub-committee of the date of the next meeting of the Council and also to point out that as the asylum was for the use of the whole county the Council was of the opinion that the sewage should be dealt with by the Asylums Board ; ard that to fix any cost of the disposal of the sewage on the Parish or Winwick would he unreasonable, as W;nwick was contributing towards , Rainhill and other Asylums.

NEVER was a more pain- The Duty of the ful duty imposed upon a Allies.

number of allied Powers than that which confronts Europe, America, and Japan at the present moment. There is no escape from the obligations they owe to each other to combine for the punishment of the rebels and their leaders at Pekin, whetiaer their leaders in- clude the Empress and her advisers or not. An awful crime has been penetrated rare in the annals of the world, and possible,we should have thought, only for the lowest of the African tribes on the West Coast,and certainly not expected from Chinese rulers and generals. The ignorant Boxers cannot estimate correctly the power of the foreigners against whom they have declared a war of exter- mination. The Mandarins and the Viceroys, the Royal family and their generals, can be under no weak illusions on the point. They knew the wrath they would excite,the extent of the strength of the POwers they have defied, and the probable course of a conflict in which the hordes of the East threw themselves against the disciplined battalions of the West. Their criminality is of the deepest dye. It cannot be excused either by patriotism or by fanaticism. The Powers have one immediate duty before them—to get posses- sion of Pekin, and, if possible, the dynastic heads and leaders. The Chinese army opposes us with the newly-added resources of military science, and with soldiers apparently trained in the latest movements and devices. The Boxers, as such,can- not be highly trained, unless the movement has invaded the ranks of the army, has been enemur.. aged by its chiefs, and has extended to all the army reserves in the northern province. To beat back these forces that bar the way to Pekin is the first duty of the time. The season is not favour- able to military operations, the district has been artificially flooded, the railway has been destrnYedg and the Chinese forces probably outnumber the .se of the Allies by four to one. Stich da- culties must be faced. Now that the foreigners in Pekin have been overwhelmed in one common destruction, a little delay does not matter. As reinforcements arrive, the Allieg will be better able to make it impossible for the, Chinese to make any impression on Tientsin, au* to repair and guard the railway. Even if the 001 Japanese force should advance on Pekin by au independent route, Tientsin must be strongly held• The fate of Pekin itself is of some interest. 0 may be destroyed before we can roach it. We We to deal with a cunning and treacherous foe,and v 46 must expect no military advantages that are sob won by military strength. The Royal Family DAY fly into the interior, and the Boxers may attemP.t to destroy the capital. If they leave it intact, It may be the duty of the Allies to decide what is tc) be the fate of a capital bloodstained with suell awful memories. It is recommeaded in Ger" many and France that Pekin should be razed to the ground. This may be neither Wise practical, nor humane. But Ptkin cannot anY, longer be the capital. It must be transferrea to some place more accessible from the sea, arid more directly under the e Jay control of the Powerg: Beyond this point we cannot advance as yet. IL the ringleaders in the massacre can be caugh° they will have to be dealt with firmly asa judiciously,either by exile and imprisonment,or 11 some more summary process. In the meantinle/ we must strongly reinforce the army of the All'eg„ at Tientsin, prepare for outbreaks elsewhere, chez' the shipment of any incomplete orders from Euree and elsewhere, and band our energies to what 10 great task—the punishment of the guilty, °II° salvation of China from anarchy, and the enthrosr ment of an Emperor or Rsgent from whom lie may expect obedience to treaties and respect for 31/ I the rights of the interested Powers.

div.p: lzornent. There has been only one real moment Of this kind, and that was when LORD ROBERTS had entered Pretoria. Ever since then there have been minor mishaps, much uncertainty, and no Play for psychological , moments at all. The country is relieved to have such an Act in existence as the Septennial Act. It must be a great relief to the Govern- Mont at the present moment to think that it need not be in a hurry at all. Time favours it, if events do not. It must wait, if it be seeking for a Psychological moment, and it is compelled to go ou because the law favours the process. The Septennial Parliament is not an institution we admire. Events outgrow opinions, and majorities Cease to correspond with political views. At pre- sent it is a relief to know that there need be no quest of the kind indicated. The Government has Only to remain as it is until next year is out, and We question whether it would be compelled to elect a new Parliament until the end of May, 1902. -hence it can contemplate with indifference what 18 being said about the importance of catching the Public mind in the right state of gratitude, appre- hension, or bewilderment. This would be to fix Upon a state of things likely to benefit the party ul power, even if its work were uncompleted and. full of gaps and puzzles. The ordinary statutory arrangement is bAter than this looking out for an oPening, but, of course, it is compatible with a decision that the better plan is to dissolve before Alay, 1902. The psychological moment, in this ease, will be completed work and a rounded-off appeal. But this is not quite the same thing as trusting to a temporary attitude of the public mind Which might change in a month or so.

Runcorn (Urban District) population at census 1891-20,050 ; estimated population in middle of 1899-19,000 These significant figures we take from Dr. MeDougall's report to the Cheshire County Council, and the obvious conclusion to be derivod fro n them is that Runcorn, as a town and community, is in a parlous state: Nine years of Uninterrupted prosperity in the country generally, the advent of the Snip Canal with its attendant Commerce, and yet the population of a town so favourably situated as Runcorn is, has, instead of Increasing, decreas..d by 1,050. Tne Medical Officer of Health attributes it to the "depressed state of trade locally," and he is unquestionably correct in his judgment. This decrease of popu- lation is a very serious matter—more serious than the great majlrity of the people concerned realise—and it behoves them to bear it in mind. Perhaps our correspondent who pens "Runcorn Notes" has overlooked its significance, for he is ever urging the local authority to spend with a freedom hardly justified by the commercial pros- perity of the town, however much it is called for by the needs of the public. It must always be a question of expediency with the Urban Council, Who have to make ends meet whatever happens, and the difficulty of doing so is not lessened by Runcorn's obvious—we hope only temporary— Commercial decay. raere are many enterprising, long-headed men in the town and we have some faith in their ability to get the good ship " Run- Corn over the bar. It wdl take time, but per- severance and pluck have succeeded in the face of greater difficulties. A word of counsel to those inhabitants who want everything doing at once /nay Dot be out of place. Let them have patience and put their shoulders to the wheel.

A medical journal has lately cast doubt on ono 'of the oldest traditions of the human race. The belief that before drowning a person rises to the tnrface of the water three times is cherished in "ery household. Its use iS essential to the re- in describing any heroic rescue demanding vue attention of the Royal Humane Society. "As tle Was about to sink for the third time "We 'avo.all read it, and wondered at the callousness ot the observer in taking count at such a moment instead of running for help. The medical theory is quite different. 'lt is that the human body will float quite naturally on water, and the question of sinking depends on the amount of liquid absorbed •when the suffirer is on the top. This fills the lungs, and adds to the weight. The real cause of a non-swimmer's difficulty is nervousness, which 'causes struggling, and makes it next to impossible for him to lie on his bacg. When the weight of Clothes is added the case becomes a very trying one, although a little knowledge of a few elemen- tary strokes will prolong the chanc.s of rescue. The marvellous thing is that the inhabitants of this sea-girt island should have paid so little atton- •tion to the art, an! that, indeed, it should not have 'been included among the compulsory subjects for -all healthy children. The notion of some sailors that to learn swimming is a mockery, because the ability will lengtben out the agony in the event of •'4ahipwreck, is, absurd. The way in which so many strong swimmers have been saved is sufficient to 'Contradict the theory as affecting the average Chance.

TEM meeting held at Lord sTweedmouth'i on Tuesday to promote a memorial to Mrs. Gladstone, While not appealing directly for financial assist- ance to the netion at large, is deserving of atten- tion,because of the tributes offered to the deceasad lady. The conveners of the gathering included Mr. Baltour and Mr. ,Goschen, a proof, if any were 'needed, that the regard for the great statesman's Wife stretched far beyond his immediate political 'Circle. In the qualities associated with the life .Companions of Prime Ministers e idler in the cen- tury Mrs. Gladstone failed completely. In fact, he allowed judgment to go bv default. She took Qlo interest whatever the salon, and so far from assisting her husband by the promotion of social lissemblies she discouraged them by eery means In her power. Her ambition was donsesticity•—to ilecure for the tireless worker freedem of mind from all the fatigues of his daily work as soon as his w. irk was ended. Yet in the small dinner parties from which he could disenmage him- self as easily as from the family circle Mr. Glad- stone was enabled by his wife to get a great deal of knowledge of persons, and there is no doubt that the hostess, in selecting many of the guests, largely distributed the ecclesiastical, jodical and other appointments which fell within Mr. .Glad- stone's disposal. It was the pride of both that these were for the most part free of any political bias, and numbers of Conservatives had reason to testlfy to Mr. Gladstona's austere sense of hiere- spousibility to the nation in these matters. In some instances the choice was not justified bvex- Perience, but in placing character before ability it Was inevitable that some dull people ehould tee Made eminent.

According to Mr. R. A. Naylor, there is a serious nuisance arising from a brook at Thelwall, and for some time be has been making life miserable for the Rural Councillors of Runcorn who are the authority controlling the district. They have been bombarded with letters full of gruesome detail 3 of Pestilence and death, and when they unwisely )aughed at the complaint they were severely -ehided by the complainant who has at last pre- vailed upon them to visit the site aid judge for themselves. Messrs. Long's tannery was suspected causinc, the unissnce, but the report of the CGunty Medical OFficnr, leaves the guilt of the tannery not proven. More remarkable still how- ever, it ascribes much of the nuisance to the sew- go from some 20 cottages which are owned by the indignant sufferer, Mr. R. A. Naylor, who has been served with a notice to abate the nuisance °Y the delighted District Council. There is some- thing very amusing in this little incident to those 1111.0 have read Mr. Nayler's complaints. He Painted the case very black indeed, and now finds °loch of his condemnation recoiling upon himself. 4e the County Medical Officer is a disinterested fersonage Mr. Naylor will have to be satisfied with "e verdict and extract as much pleasure as P°esinle from abating the nuisance at his own ex- tense. He has already earned the gratitude of )01.11 villagers, and bids fair to earn that of the tstrict Council also.

When cyclists here possess the privileges and powers of their brethren in Epperor William's fatherland they may rightly deem themselves a fortunate class of persons. In Germany a magis- trate has committed to prison a pedestrian who recklessly ran across the street and upset a cyclist. In this free and enlightened country the cyclist would probably come in for the punish- ment after having had to answer num- berless questions concerning the speed he was going at, whether he rang his bell, the dimensions of his gear, whether he used Globe Polish for his handlebar, and other equally pertinent particulars. You can't anathematise your Emperor in Germany but you can, if you are a cyclist, do many things which would cause trouble here. And this is some compensation for being forbidden the first-named sweet privilege. The N.C.U. might import a few magistrates of the type officiating in Germany just to teach pedestrians, and juveniles who dash suddenly out of back passages, that the streets are for the cyclists and not for their ignoble trouble- some selves.

A Provincial Letter.

A moment's reflection will show how materially the working classes in this country, and especially in the provinces, are affected by what is happening in China. England, Japan, and the United States are the people most closely related, commercially in the order named; and so long as the presnt crisis may last there must ff be much suerin Te g. e i stoppage of manufactures n Lancashire has already been announced, as shipments of manufac•ured goods for China have temporarily, ceased. Japan ioked to China for her future living, so to speak, in the way of:sea-borne trade and. a market for her rising manufactures. American trade with China is of very old standing, as ancient, in fact, as the history of the States themselves Germany had just selected China as the first place on weich she should plant her foot as the "world-power." Russian trade with China is, for the most part, carried on by the old caravan routes, gradually supplemented by railway facilities. Her commercial dealings would be little disturbed by whatever happened. Everywhere people had been complaining of the absence of summer weather, and the prospect of being deprived of their usual holiday. But here we are, in the dog days•tnly,with the thermometer ai; near a hundred d-grees in the SIM, one day after another. Shooting in the various events at Daley on one day of the week was carried on with a solar temperature of 149 in the sun, with 80 in the shade anu on the following day 142.2 in the sun. This is more than even summer holiday-makers cared for, and has had the effect of keeping most of them within doors during the day. Monday is said to have been the hottest day hitherto of the year, and none of us want it any warmer.

Agricultural journals have collected their first returns as to the condition of the farm crops ot Great Britain. The reports are on the whole favour- able, toe cold and droughty spring having been followed by showers in the latter half ofJurte. While the condition of tne wheat crop is inferior to•that of a year ago, tne state of the barley is better,and that of oats considerably better. Grass crops of allkinds, including both grazing lauds and hay fields, work Out far better than last year, when they were seri- ously handicapped by the drought of June. In a dozen Eng Lien ceunties the average of the root crep islower tuan last year,but:the general position is fa. superior to that of last July, wnich, if one takes it as an observant outsider,is saying much. In the annual Parliamentary "Massacre of the inuocenca " this week figures tne Dogs' Bill. This Bill, curiously enough, arouses sentiments in the provinces, particularly among the farming classes, of as bitter a kind as are aroused, at any rate out- eide Parliament, by any Bill brought before the two Elouses this session. Yet it is a well-intentioned and moderate measure, framed with a view to rounding off Mr. Walter Long's successful and marl- curious achievements in the direction of banishing irom tnis country the horrible disease of hydro- phobia. The severity of Mr. Long's doe-muzzling policy has been generally condemned by dog-, ewners, of course, but the Minister of Agriculture, I when interrogated on the subject, has been in the nappy position to reply that only one case of rabies had occurred to the end of July last year through- ' out England, and that the practical stamping out of the disease would alone enable him to issue instruc- tions for the general revocation of the order. Even' the owners of dogs should hail such an order as one i of more than mere relief, as something indeed to be proud of and grateful for nationally. A table show- ing the number of counties of Great Britain in which cases of rabies in dogs were reported.in each year from 1895 to July 25th of last year, gives the following remarkable results: 1895,coanties 29,cames 672; 1896, counties 41, cases 438; 1897. counties 30. cases 157: 1898,counties 10,cases 17; 1899(to July 25)1 counties one, cases one. In these days of excessive heat of course, especial care should be taken to ' multiply as far as possible the facilities afforded to dogs to drink clean fresh water. In some towns dog troughs are fairly plentiful, while in others they appear to be seldom thought of. in the smaller towns and villages they might be multipliel with advantage for the relief of dogs passing through with conveyances. So much has this dog muzzling question taken possession of the minds of men in the provinces, that if a general election 11.0 be,ai brought about several months since, it would ,undoubtedly have materially affected the voting in 'many of the Parliamentary divisions. Whether it would do so now may well be doubted ; notwith- standing the bitterness of feeling that has been causel. Reminders in the papers of cat owners wile leave their pets to the mercy of a eat-despising world while they are away on health or pleasure bent have become quite a "hardy annual." It is well knownhow little are appreciated,by most of us, those things that cost us least. A cat costs noth- ing, as a rule, the owner of the kitten being only too glad to get rid of it and its toe numerous brotners and sisters, from its birth. But, provided always that the receiver will " take every care" of the interesting stranger. Nor does its maintenance cost much more, except it be like some that one cent(' mention which have lost their instinct for hunting the "small deer' of our kitchen and pantry, from over indulgence in riotous living. These pampered creatures ought assuredly to be taxed, together with all those that make the night hideous; but the difficulty of dealing with the res- pectable tabby who earns her own living,and of ap- peasing her feminine owner,has hitherto prevented this. Even when left alone for a few days, there are those cats that will contrive to pick up a living and some that go away occasionally on their own account and come back after several days, 89 fat and sleek as before. But the pampered ones are really to be pitied,and their owners should be made. to pay a tax, Fewer cats and " paying " cats, are things to be desired in very many neighbouriioade ' genteel certainly included. The first half of the present year appears to have been much more disastrous to the building trade than was the corresponding period of 1899. There have been, in the six months just ended. 203 re- ceiving orders gazetted, against 154 in the first half of last year. Grocers come next with 154 failures, against 160,and publicans with 133 failures, againet 160. Out of a total of 2,217 receiving orders, these three classes of trade account for 495 Farmers made up a list of 92 failures, as compared with 86, and then came butchers, eigh'y-two,against eighty- one. Decorators,bakers. boot and shoe traders, and drapers all number 50 to 60 in the list, and then we come gradually down to the most solvent people who appear to be leather factors, and smack- owners. -

.13,,Pr measure spells " queer measure " in thos3 parts of the country where what is known as the "long pull "is or has been in vogue, By the long pull is meant a pull at the beer-engine of more beer than the quantity asked or suppo;ed to be paid for. The tride in the Black Country have taken the matter in hand, but the gain may he considered one for the temperance party as well, and, it appears to be succeedinv, It, CAME) into operation on 31.mday, and really means that not more than twenty-five per cent. more out-supply beer must be allowed than asked for.

CITELL AMONGST TFIN GOATS

Frederick Chell, greengrocer, a well-known character of Runcorn, made his 3311 appearance be- fore the Runcom Bench, on fhursAy morning, to answer to a charge of drunk and disorderly on the previous day.—According to Constable Gilpin, who proved the case,Cheil was in a state of intoxication in Halton-roau, and a,saulting almost every- body that passed down that way. Gilpin took him in hand, pacified him a little. and got him into a house. This did not suit Chell at all, for he came out of.the house minas his coat an i vest, and with his braces hanging down,and "wen: for"cwo young goats, which were in the road, and which he stated "he would do for" as they were the Cause of the row. Gilpin seeing Chell abuse the poor animals took him in custody and lolged him in the Police cells.—Chell, whose face was very much discoloured, said it was all due to family affairs, his brother-in-law had struck him as they could not agree,—The .51agistrate : No, it is not. You get drunk, and it makes you like a madman.— The Superintendent observed there were not many publicans in the town who would serve any liquor to Chet!, but somehow he bad managed to get it.— Prisoaer was committed to linntsford fr a month.
RUNCORN NO rEs. [By A CORRESPONDENT].

Mr. C. E. Linaker may not have ben exactly right in maintaining that tile District Councillor was a nobody outside his official capacity, but it is pleasing to note that the majority of the District Councillors declined to accept the duties of a "sub- nuisance inspector," which would have undoubtedly fallen to their lot had Almiral Jones Parry suc- ceeded iii passing his motion. With all due respect to the Admiral it must be said, his intention of the clause was for the District Councillor of each parish to be acquiainted with what was going ; but obviously the moaon as moved by him wou.,d only incline to invest the District Councillor with a position whica would be invidious; and, surely,tha. is a state which even th-4 Admiral doas not desire.

The fining of a Halton publican for -permitting drunkenness, which the ituncora Bench decided upon at the Sessions on Nfonday, is very satisfac- tory. It is encouraging to the potice, and encourag- ing to all classes desirous of emancipating human depravity. Drunkenness is caused by the imbibing of too much alcoholic liquor; and, notwithstanding the advancement of " open air theories," implies " supplying to an excessive extent "on the part ot someone. If that "supplying to an exceisive ex- tent "is not making drunk, let alone permitting drunkenness, lam very much mistaken, and I should like to see a publican proceeded against every time a drunken man was found, Tai would especially conduce to the reduction of the " incap- ables "and would also tend to make publicans as a class more cireum,pact. What do our temperance reformers say on the subject ?

It may be calculated, by some people, that from my allusions to health matters ( which have been pretty numerous for the past week,), I would c3n- stitute myself into a kind of Assistant Medical Officer of Health, or Nuisance Inspector, or, may be some will incline to the belief that I would even fain be Consulting Surveyor; or, indeed, all three combined. Such office, however, I decline to presume to. Yet, would I emphasise the point that, if a layman in such matters can see all that to which I have already given voice.; surely, those whose business it is to look into things ought to see more ; and, further, up in them there should rest the additional responsibility of finding a cure. It is though, pleasing to see the cep the health Committee have taken by the issue of their latest warning respecting the deposit of refuse in the streets. It is a step in the right direction ; and, if followed up vigorously, will prove productive of good.

Our fellow townsman, Chell, upon whose behalf I appealed some weeks ago, has again fallen a victim to drink and the Police, and now languishes in Knutsford Gaol. me police find, and I can verify it by considerable experience, that Chell is all right when unpossessed by "the demon drink," and a general request has been issued—and indeed as to a great extent been complied with—that. the Run- corn publicans do not serve him with any intoxic- ants. Notwithstanding this appeal, however,Chell has got "within the measur.v" more than once, and to those people, who perhaps were unwittingly re- sponsible for it, I would strongly appeal again to assist in making the man a "compulsory teetotaler" for the credit of the town.
I RUNCORN RURAL DISTRIC.%#T COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting ot the Council was held at Dutton Worklll,ise, on Tuesday atteracon. There were pr.sent :—Mr J KIOWiI33 (chairman), Mr S Woodward (vice-cbairtnari),Adlniral Jone -Parrr,Messrs J Mclntyre E Clarke, T Lewis, C E Linker, T Wright, J Moseley- Williams, T Darlington, E Bretherton, P °leave, G Pilling, r Ant wiss. J B Chadwick, with Mr George F Ashton (clerk), Mr W E Hough (deputy clerk), Messrs Diggle and Swinton (surveyors), James Farrington (inspector), and Dr. Joseph Adams (medical officer).

NO NEED FOE COMPLAINT. /dr. RNinald Potts,clerk to the County Council,wrote under date 11th sir,—Nuisance arising from ditches by the side of main roads.—The County Surveyor informs me that a nuisance is occasioned by sewage being permitted to be turned into tbe ditch by the aide of tne main road aiongaide them:thy at Sutton Weaver and that the same is injurious to the health of the persons requiring to use the main road at that point. I shall be obliged, therefore, if you will bring this matter under the notice of your District Council at the earliest opportunity with a view to the same being immediately rem ,ved ."

The Inspector thought it was impossib!e for a nuis- ance to exist there and gave it as his opinion there was no nuisance injurious to health. Mr. Linaker and Mr. S. Woodward agreed with the view taken iby the Inßoector, the latter affirming he had never smelt any effilvia arising therefrom, and the most he had seen was a little deposit of soap suds. (Laughter.) The Clerk was instructed to reply that the Inspec- tlr of Nuisances did not consider it a nuisance danger- ous to health. STOCKTON HEATH'S OBJECTIONS TO THE PROPOSED LIGHT
RAILWAY SCHEME.

Mr. E. Bradshaw, clerk to the Parish Council of S,ockton Heath, f3rwarded a copy of the Council's ob- jectioas to the proposed Warrington and Runcorn Light ttailcvay, and was instructed t 3 ask that tbe District Coußeit would assisc, the Parish Council in opposing the scoerne.—The Palish Ccuacil considered that the road should be widened to at least 40 feet from kerb to kerb before the scheme could be entertained. The objections were (1) that the road proposed to be traversed is too narrow for the purpose; (2) that there is no provision fer loading or unloading texcep':, in the public street ; (3) that no regulation as regards speed is inserted in he Bid : (4) t'aat the value of prop3rty will be depreci- ated; (5) coat the railway will be a source of danger to life.
The letter was referred to the PArliamentary Com- inittoe on the proposition of Mr. S. Woodward seconded by Mr. Ge )rge Pilling. "DISTRICT COUNCILLORS" NOT" INSPECTORS OF NUISANCE !'

Admiral Jones Parry propmi "that in future the Councillors for the parish in which a nuisance arises,and the Medical Officer of Health shall b 3 notified of all cc.:l-1- plaints of nuisance within the district of the Council ; toe Medical Officer of Health shall immediately upon re- clving such notice enquire into the circumstances of the case, and give such instruc,tions as he may deem necesiary to the Inspector of Nuisances, who shall keep nim informed of all action taken thereon. The Modica Officer of Health shall also report thereon to the COURCi at their next meeting following the receipt of the notice -ind at each succeeding meeting until any such nuliance which may exist, has been abated." In doing so be observed it was the outcome of difficulty hitherto ex- perienced of being able to hold someone responsible. Mr. E. Clarke seconded.

Mr. C. E. Linaker was sorry he could not support the Admiral. Flowever desirable it was for the Medical Officer and the Inspector to work hand in hand, he thought it was better to keep District Councillors out of anything of the sort. Out;ide the Council Chamber he contended the District Councillor was a nonentity. He would not oppose the resolution if the clause referring to the District Counctlhr was deleted ; but if a councillor of any district was t 3 be drawn in as a kind of sub- nuisance inspector, he would certainly oppose it. It was no use them having offiaials if they had to do their work.
Admiral Parry contended that hA had no wish to take away any power of the Medical Offi,.:er or Inspector. Fie aimed at the Dis:rict Councillor being notified of what w is going on.

L'n-lker further contended that knowledge could be acquired by the fortnightly visit to Dat.ton, and attention to the business ; and also even supposing such a roolution was passed it was within the province of the Meal Officer and Inspector to ignore the District Cluncillors outside the Council. If they esereised their power as a CJuncil well and good, but be did object to individualism. The motion was lost only two voting for it.
THE EHPLLYMENT OF ROADMEN AS HARVESTERS.

Admiral Parry proposed " first in future the Sur• veyors of the highways be empowered either on applica- tion from, or with the consent of the District Councillor for the Parish in which the man works, to allow any road min under his control to be hired by farmers during harvest time."

Mr. Linaker azaia opposed oa the same principle as the previous resolution. It was, however, ultimately pointed out by the chair- man, that the labourers were so employed at the discretion of the surveyors, who engaged their own men as they required them. The discussion subsequently ceased.
TUE TIIELWALL NUISANCE. ACTION DECIDED UPON.

Further letters were read from Mr. Naylor, Cuerden Hall, Warrinzton, in one of which he declined to act on the Commite3 appointed, as amongst other reasons "he wished clearly and distinctly to sit tte that it was not a personal or unfriendly matter b.tween himself and his neighbour. Mr. Long, but entirely a question of public health." A. tet:er was read from Mr Long intimatiog that he or another numb )r of the firm would meet the Committee and. go over the Tannery with them.

The Committee app -Anted to consider the matter, renorted they met at the site of the alleged nuisance, at 3.45 p.m. on Wednesday, the 11% last, when there were present :—Megsra Darlineton, Monte- field, Pilling, Mclntyre, Knowles, Admiral J P Jones-Parry, Dr Vacher (county medical officer of health), Dr Adams (district medical officer of health), Mr Joseph Farrington (inspector of nuisaneds) and Mr George F Ashton (clerk). The committee were met by Mr Long, the owner of the Tannery, who fully explained the various Processes through which the hides passed in the course of their manufacture into leather.and allowed the Committee and Medical Officers to inspect all pasts of the works. He contended that the nuisance created arose from sewage from Mr. Naylor' and other houses which emptied into the brook. The Committee and Medical Officers made a thorough inspection of the works and brook, and the County Medical Officer of Health stared that he would forward his report to the Clerk. The County Medical Officer, in the course of an ex- haustive report on the subject, was of epinion that the owners of the land on which the foul ditch and tank were situated might be proceeded against under section 91 (sub-section 2) and required to abate the nuisance forthwith. The owners of the 20 houses or cottages polluting thii brook were, he was of opinion, committing an offeece against the Rivers Pollution Prevention Act, and they might be proceeded against and required to cease pollutine the broik with crude sewage. The owners of the Tannery might aso be proceeded against. provided the Council found onlanalysis that their present (-.7 sent did not come up tithe required standsrd of pniisy,. If all the polluting material was taken out of the water- course by the road side, as 5t should be, no nuisance would arise there from, and there would be no ocmsion to pipe it. In reply to the Chairman Dr. Adams stated be had nothing to add to Dr. Varther'a report. After some discussion Mr. Woodward moved that Mr. Naylor be reqnested to abate the nuisance arising from his cottages, anrithat steps be taken to analyse the effluent from theannery. and that all other persons who contributed to the nuisnce be ordered to remedy the matter.
Mr. T. Wright secocdod, and it was unanimously agread to.
THE POLLUTION OF Et&TTON BROOK.

The Clerk read the report of the committee appointed to consider the question of the pollution of Hatt on Brook by thesewage of the parish of Eltaton The com- mittee meta committee of the Corporation of Warring- ton with reference to the pollution of this brook and the consequent injuira to the waterworks of the Corpora- tinn on the 27th June. when there were present Messrs. Bixter, D trington. Mawdsley, and Bradford, together with the Clerk and Surveyor representing the Council and six members of the Corporation together with the Town Clerk and Water Engineer of Warrington. The Warrin?- ton Eurrineer produced a scheme by which the sewage could be taken from the present outfall to a point below the site of the new reservoir proposed to br constructed by the Corporation there to be located in settling tanks and then tereed into Rosewood Brook, at a total cost of about £7OO The mernbers of the Corporation then offered teat if this scheme were carried out they would be willing to contribute £2OO to- wards the cost. After some discussion the Council's Committee agreed to consider the ccherne and meet again on the 11th of July.—The committee visited the site of the proposed works on the 6th of July when there were present Messrs B txter, Darlington, and Mawdsley, together with the Clerk and Surveyor, also Mr White and Mr Smith Burgess, agents to Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. Mr White informed the committee that Sir Gilbert would not agree to the effluent from the filter beds going into Resewold Brook at the point named by the Corporation Engineer and pointed out another site on the east side of the road which he thought would be a more suitable position for the settling tanks and which he stated Sir Gilbert would allow the Council to take at a nominal rent. The committee agreed to the site and instructed the Surveyor to prepare plans and estimates of a scheme in time for the meeting with the Corpora- tion on the 11th of July--The committee met the com- mittee of the Corporation on the 11th of July when there were present Messrs Baxter, Darlington, and IMawdsley together with the Clerk and Surveyor repre•

seating the Council.and five members of the Corporation ' with the Town Clerk and Water Engineer. The ccm- -1 imittee of the Council submitted their scheme to the Committee of the Corporation and informed them that they were prepared to make the flltec beds at a cost of about £2OO if the Corporation would bear the expense of laying the pipes from the present outfall to the site of alp proposed beds which was estimated to cost £360. After some discussion the Committee of the Corporation agreed t ) carry out the suggestion provided the Council obtained the necessary wayleaves and undertook that all sewage should be taken out of the brook." Mr. Dirlington who proposed that the report of the committee be adopted, said it was their opinion that tney had made a very good bargain. Mr. Woodward Lecended and the motion was agreed to.

When the wine is in the wit is oat," is a well- known axiom, but Samuel Fielding, a seaman of the "Liberty" now lying at Old Docks, Runcorn,proveil the exception. Having at about 11.300 n Wednes- day night, reached a state of liquorous hilarity he took to the amusing diversity of chasing a dog. Whilst the fun was at its height Constable Edwards appeared on the scene Bad in turn chased the dog chaser; tue sequel to which was tee appearance of both before tile Runcorn Bench, on Thursday morning, and Fielding was fined .5s including Costs. FIRE AT LEE STREET, WIDNES.

An alarming fire broke out in a house situate in Lee-street, occupied by Daniel McKeon, a labourer, on Pridav .night. A tank containing three gallons of paraffin oil szoad under the stairs, and there was also a lot of paper and rubbish. The little son,ao.l three years, was observed corninz from the place with b. piece of lighted paper in his hand. shortly afterwards Mrs. McKeon heard a crackling noise, and upon going towards the stairs she discovered them to be on fire. Water was thrown upon the flames, and in about fifteen minutes the bitize was extinguished. The stairs, doors, and doorposts were much burned, the damage being estimated at about £lO. Tao prompt action taken alone prevented disastrous consequences. THE CAPTURE OF DESERTERS IT WIDNES.

John Carney and Robert Cuardau were charged b.tfore the Widnes Magistrates on Nioaday last with deserting from the Ist Battalion Royal North Lan- cashire Regiment, :;stationed at Fulwood Barracks, Preston,.ou the llch inst.—P.C. Worst°ld stated that on the .pravious day, in the alterunon, he noticed the defendants acting suspiciously in Victoria-road. He questioned them, an 1 their answers were rather confusing. He puiled one of the defendants trousers up and saw that he was wearing military socks. They denied that they had deserted. Witness brought them to the police station and found that the other man was wearing military braces. Here they said "Itis no use tell- ing lies, you have 'copped' us; we have deserted."— Defendants were eacn remanded to await an escort and a reward of• 15. s eaca was allowed the officer.

CHOIR SERMONS AT S. MICHAEL'S, RUNCORN. The annual sermons on behalf of the choir were preached on Sunday. At the morning service psalms were sung to Havergal and Foster, and the Te Daum to Simper. A very appropriate sermon dealing .with thanksgiving, was preached by the Rev U D Wray, M.A., vicar of Halton. In the after- noon a flower service was held in the church con- ducted by the Rev E S Oliver, assistant curate,Run- corn. There was a very good attendance, and gifts of choice flowers were contributed,these afterwards being distributed among the sick poor in the neighboarhood. At evensong the psalms were sang to Baruby, Woodward, and Russell, and the cantata aad the Dens Miserea,tur to Vincent. The anthem, " The Lord is,King," by Trimnsl, was admirably rendered by the choir, the quartette being taken by Masters P Ridge and J Hill, and Messrs J Blundell and %V Hopwood. The singing both morning and evening was exceptionally good, the boys having been specially trained by Mr C Pownall. Mr. Grounds presided at the organ. The collections through the day realised considerably over £ll, which is an excellent advance on previous years. CLAIM AGAINST THE LONDON AND NORTH- WESTERN RAILWAY CgIIKPANY AT WIDNES.

On Friday, at the Widnes County Court, before his Honour Judge Collier, %Pill Ham Cooper. Terrace- road, Widn&4, tent sail maker, claimed £3 103 from the London and North-Western Railway Company for delay in the delivery of a tent from Widnes to Dunham Hill, for use at a fête on May 16th.—Mr. Loraine, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr Fauna) appeared for the company.—The plaintiff said he had sent these things to Dunham Hill for May 15th. Some of them arrived in time,and some did not get there until the 19th. In consequence they were no use for the lila). The Rev Stullito, who was concerned in the gathering, refused to pay the amount of money for the things as they did not reach there in time—Mr. Loraine admitted that some of the goods did not arrive until the 191. He said no notice wai ever given that they were required for a particular purpose,and therefore they were not liable in law for damages which were not in the contemplation of the parties at the time. He quoted several cases bearing on the subject.—His honour held that the company were not liable. MILTON WID NES. —PRES NT.LTION TO Miss JANET RELY.

There W.lB a fairly good gathering at the meeting of this brotherhood on Sunday afternoon, when Mr. T. Harrison occupied the chair, and gave some use- ful advice on' Help The sal 9ists Mr. G. Lacky, who sang 'O, brother, life's journey is begin- nine' and Miss Ilulme, "the Better Land,' each acquitted themselves satisfactorily, and gaimed hearty appreciation from the members. The Preii- dent (the Rev. J Pedlar) gave a vary lucid address on "The Umbrella and the Book." The subject was suggested by the presentation to Miss Janet fteay, the accompanist, who is leaving the town to fulfil an engagement with Joshua Dyson's Gipsy Choir of an umbrella and a book entitled"Bogatzky'e Golden Treasury." as a token of esteem and a small tribute in recognition of the valuable services she had rendered to the P.S.A. The President, in making the presentation, said that an umbrella could be utilized for two purposes, to shelter from the sun and also from rain, which was also a symbol of life, showing that life was not all sunshine, and they might have troubles and crosses,but if they trusted in Christ,and looked to Him for support and shelter' they would be all right. The book was one which it was hoped might be a help to her in ber daily life. He urged upon all the necessity of daily in- tercession and meditation, assuring them it would be a great help to them all. The remarks were meant to apply to all the members, and the class appreciated them fully. DAMAAIINO- PROPERTY IT WIDNES.

Before the Mayor of Widnes and other magis- trates, on Monday a youth named Herbert Ellis was summoned for committing damage to property -in Lugsdale-road, belonging to the United Ceeshire and Lancashire Permanent Building r3ociety, on the previouo day.—Defendant pleaded guilty.—? C. Jones said at 7 o'clock on the previous night he wai on duty in Lugsd.ale road in company with In- spector Strickland. They heard a noise in an un- occupied house. Witness went upstairs and saw the defendant and another boy pulling the laths and plaster from the ceiling. He caught the de- fendant bat the other boy jumped through the window.—Mr. Beech said he repaired the premises for the property owners. The damage committe to the eeiling amounted to £2 or .E 2 103. About a month ago they secured the windows and doors firmly by using doors from other houses, but these had been broken down. The depredators had made a way out of one house into another, under the stairs. The houses had been empty four years. His experience was that property generally in the town lad been d,maged.—Defeniant said he was looking for a nest. dr. A. Lightburn explained that that was only one in a number of serious cases. They had a case in which damage to the extent of £5 wa.s committed. It was very difficult for the police to effect a capture, as they were watched vary keenly. He was instructed to press the charge.— Inspector Strickland also gave evidence pointing out that the other lad, who got away, juniped from the bedroom window into the yard.—The Bench inflice 1 a fine of 103 and costs together with .£1 damage. They also sanctioned the refunding of the costs of the summons to the society.

div.head: .—.....,.,...,rris A RUNCORN FOOTBALLER DROWNED IN THE DEE.
div.p: .—.....,.,...,rris A RUNCORN FOOTBALLER DROWNED IN THE DEE.

Quite a gloom was cast over Runcorn on Monday evening when news was received that Mr. Alfred Taylor, landlord of the Whea sheaf Inn, Bridge-street, and a popular member of the Runcorn football team had met his death by drowning at Chester. It appears that Mr. Taylor was accompanied by several of his triends,Messrs Evan Vernon. 76, Union-street, Rancorn : Charles Henry Nixon, 1, Fisher-street, Runcorn ; and George Sefton,l2, Cooper-street.liuncorn, and that they hired a large punt in The Groves, and proceeded for a row up the river. When opposite the Grosvenor Park one of the oarsmen met with a mishap to his oar, whereupon the boat gave a heavy lurch, and capsized. The accident was witnessed by several boatmen, who as speedily as possib:e rowed to the spot, and succeeded in rescuing Vernon, Nixon, and Sefton. Taylor had disappeared several times, bat by means of a drag he was recovered in the course of a few minutes. None of the men could swim. Drs. Roberts and Giffen, of Boughton, were summoned, but all efforts to restore Taylor failed, and his body was re- moved to the mortuary to await an inquest. The decea.sed had had a long and hofiourable connec- tion with the Runcorn Rugby Football Club, having seen many years of useful service in the forward rank. He trained his county cap for Cheshire in the old Rugby Union, as well as under the Northern Union. He had the honour of belonging to the team in 1896, which carried off the Northern Union Championship, and also figured among the players last season when they again secured the much-coveted cup and medal. He leaves a widow and two children to mourn his loss, with whom much sympathy is expressed.

div.head: Dee Vindicated by the Coroner.
div.p: The Dee Vindicated by the Coroner.

Mr. E. Brassey, the Chester coroner, held an inquest at the Town Hall. Chester, on Tuesday afternoon, on the body of Alfred Taylor, 27, bricklayer, and landlord of th 3 Wheat Sheaf Inn, Bridge-street, Runcorn, who was drowned in the Dee on M)nday evening. Evidence was heard as to the circumstancas of the accident.

River Constable Jones said all the men were sober,and appeared to ha able to manage the boat, although their rowing suggested that they had been used to salt water. The Coroner said he should not have gone into the circumstances of the accident in such detail had it not been for things which had been said in Rnt a very kindly way about the way in whieti the Chester people were allowed to go on the river in boats which were incapable of holding them, or were allowed to indulge in any amount of carelessness in them, and that the Chester Dee was becoming noted as a death-trap. He had the curiosity to look up his records about the river,leeling pretty certain that what accidents did occur were due not to the overcrowding of the boats, but to the carelessness of the thausands of strangers who came to Chester full of spirit, and who knew nothing about boats, and who moved about in them as though they were train cars. Hundreds and thousands of persons in Chester used the boats in the course of a year, and yet he found that during the past five years not a single Chester person had been drowned within the jurisdiction of the city coroner, which extended from the White House right down to the wharf at Saltney. He was sure if Air. Bate, the county coroner, were to look over the returns be would find that a very large per- centage of the calamities above the city occurred to people who were strangers to Chester. The accident in question arose through the mismanagement, or inability to manage an oar of one of the four young men.
The jury returned a verdict of accidentally drowned, and concurred in the coroner's remuks as to the river. THE FUNERAL.

! The funeral of the deceased took place, on Thursday afternoon, at the Runcorn Cemetery. at which place the Rev N J Poole, curate of Holy Trinity, Runcora, per- formed the impressive burial service. 'The streets, from the deceased's residence to the Ceinetery, were literally thronged with townspeople, whom had turned out to see the last of one of their most popular inhabitants and many were the expressions of sympathy with the young wife and children, and other rela- tives of. the young athlete, who, in but his 26th year, had been so tragically summoned away. Blinds were drawn and other manifestations of heartfelt mourning were visible all along the route. div.head: RUNCOFN COMPANY'S AFFAIRS'
div.p: A RUNCOFN COMPANY'S AFFAIRS'
Standard PAetals Recovery, Limited.

The statutory meeting of the creditors and share- holders of the Staradard Metals Recovery, Limited, were held on Wednesiay at the Carey-street offices of the Board of Trade. The Company had works at Ruocern, where they carried on the extraction of arsenic by a special process. Mr. Wincaris, Aseistant Receiver, reported that the Company was formed in August, 1656, for the purpose of erecting smelting works for the treatment of complex and refractory ores, but mainly for the extraction of arsenic. The capital was fired at £10,000; but in March, 1900, it was increased by the creation of 2 ,000 six per cent, cumulative preference shares. A circular in the shape of a prospectus, and offering those shares, was sent out to a few friends of the directors, and 1,413 shares were subscribed for in response thereto. They were not allotted, however, owing to the meeting falling through in the absence of a quorum of directors, and the £1,413 was now included in the liabilities of the Company. Tao Company purchased machinery, and erected works at Runcorn, where the special process for the extraction of arsenic had been proceeded with ; but at the date of the winding up only a few tons of arsenic had been produced. An execution had been levied at the works on bohalf of Mr. Allan Gibbs the manager, and the sheriff was still in possession there' The failure of the Company was attributed by the secretary to delay in commencing work, and to break- downs in the machinery. The machinery and plant cost the Company £2,160, but it would be valeeless if the trust wore broken up, and an off.?r of £6OO which had been made for it appeared beneficial. The unsecured liabilities amounted to £2,144, and the account with the cr-clitorg and shareholders disclosed a total deficiency of £11,816. Mr. Swan, a director, intimated that steps were in progress for a reconstruc- tion of the Company, under which the sebscrib Ts for the prelereace shares would be allottzd shares in the new Company, subject to a small liability on each share, and the claims of the other creditors would be arrange I. The shareholders of the old Company excep,ing rt. e holder-; of vender's or paper shares, would also receive shares in the reconstructed Company. A resolution was Passed for the official Receiver to ect es liquidator, and to wind up the Company, assisted by a committee of inspection.

Bravery Rewarded. At a meeting of the Royal Humane Society in London on Monday a testimonial was given to Robert Thomas, Latchford, for a daring feat on June 18th, when he succeeded in saving a lunatic named Moody, who had thrown himself into the Ship Canal. In order to effect the rescue, Thomas had himself lowered down some 26 feet, He then placed a rope round Moody, who was hauled up before himself.
