div.head: LEGISLATIVE PROPOSALS.
div.p: LEGISLATIVE PROPOSALS.

The Actuary presented the following report :—ln the present Session of Parliament two bills affecting savings banks were introduced, one by the Chancellor of the Exchequer on behalf of the Government and the other by Sir Albert Rollit and others as representing the com- mittee of inspection of Trustee Savings Benke.The maim principle of the Government Bill was ceneeined ha section one, by which it was proposed that in annually determining the rates of interest payable to savings banks," the Treasury is to have regard to incomes which may be expected to accrue in the ensuing year from the investments of Savings Bank funds." Not less than one month's notice of any change was to be given to savings banks before the commencement o. the savings bank year. This has come to be known as the sliding scale proposal. The main prineiple of Sir Albert Rollit's Bill was a propesed enlargement of the area of the character of inveetnacnts allowed t ) savings bank& At present all except in the case of a very few long established savings banks, can only invest their funds with the National Debt Commissioners, and it was sought by the Bill to have the power of investing (for defined short periods) with lapel autherities on the security of the local rata?. A meeting of representatives of Trustee Savings Banks to consider these Bills was held on the 13th ult. in Lon- don and after a full discussiou it was unanimously re- selved "That in the opinion of the meeting a lower rata of interest than is now paid co savings bank depositors would not tend to encourage thrift, and that any fluc- tuations in the rate of interest as suggested in the Government Bill ie undesirable; and that in Wu thereof the range investments available to the National Debt Commissioners for savings b ,nk funds should be ex- tended to all securities permitted t i trustees under the Scotch Trust Amendment Act, 1898 wed, that in case of any chp.nge in the interest allowed by the Natiocal Dent Commieeioners not less than three menthe' notice be givers. Thee() resolutions were accompanied by a sug. geetion that the two Bills should be re.nhted to a Parlia- mentary Committee a course which tee Chencellcr c!. the Exchequer agreed to. Since then Sir M. Hicks Beach has written a letter in which he said it was a mistake to supple° that he had preff sred te reduce the rate of in- terest paid to depositors in the Post Office Saving Bank What he had proposed was that the rate of interest paid should depend on the rate earned by the deposits instead of being fixed without reference to the rate earned. This would not necessarily involve a reduction; indeed durine the greater time for whine these banks had existed it would have involved an increase, anti might possibly do so in the future. Whether the area of savings bank investments should be extended was quite another question. But, assuming it is done on the lines suggested by the memorialists,the effect in increas- ing the rates of interest carried would not be in hiS opinion as great as was anticipated, for the total amount of such securities in the market wasosmalle when compared with Consols and their merk.t price would undoubtedly be increased by the change. If local authorities wished to borrow money for the purpose of the Rousing of the Working Classes Act they eould have obtained it last year from the Public Work Loan Com- missioners at 21 per cent and though the rates were bigher just now, they would doebtless fall again te that point when the value of money falls to what it was. For the present (continued Mr Handley in his report) all danger has been averted as the government on the previous night withdrew their Bill, thus allowing more time for the formulating of well considered provisions such RS ally meet the exieencies of national finance and the encouragement of habits of thrift as evidenced by the steady growth of provident institutions' The Chairman said the Actuary had placed a very lucid stetement before them, and if necessary no doubt the Runcorn bank would join with others in dealing with a very important qeestion. At present no represents.. tion need be made, as the bills were withdrawn. On the proposition of Mr. Taylor, socce.‘d :d by Mr. Boot() a vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman for preding.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
ASSAULT ON A PAINTER.-EX-POLICEMAN IN TROUBLE.

At the Warrington Police Court on Saturday, before Messrs. T. Birchall (in the chair), and R T Fairclough, Harry Holt was charged with being drunk and disor- derly in Borough-road at 5.30 the previous evening and with assaulting Arthur Lawton at the same time.—He pleaded not guilty.—Arthur Lawton, 60, Priestley-street saiu he was a painter in the employ of the Ship Canal Company, at Stag Bridge. Prisoner was employed at the PAD:Le place. On Thursday, he and a dczin others struck work. On Friday night witness was going home in company with the foreman down New road, when he met the prisoner, who, after insulting him, struck him a vio ent blow on the head. He thought the reason why the prisoner struck him was because he would not leave his work. The men who were on strike had been Inter- fering during the day and those Nem were working had to seek police protection.—P.C.'s Baxendale and Lewis gave evidence.—Prisoner said he"nad no intention of striking the complainant. Be bad been a member of the Salford Police Force and bore a good character.—Be was fined 5s and costs for the drunkenness and 103 and costs f .r the assault.

div.head: MINOR CASES. ---- Warrington Borough Court.
div.p: MINOR CASES. ---- Warrington Borough Court.
FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair). Councillor Smethurst and Mr Heoherd

WINDow SMASHING.— William Bibby., of Warburton-street was summoned by Richard Slater Whitaker. 113, Winwick- road, for committlpg wilful damage to a window on July 6th.—Cornplainant stated that defendalit put his elbow through the window. doing damage to the amount of 156. A girl named Ellen Harrison spoke to witnessing the occurr- ence, and defendant. who did not appear was o dered to pay the amount of damage and the costs or in default go to gaol for 14 daps.
t,ATURDAY.—Before Mesars..T. Birchall (in the chair), and It.

T. Fair°lough. FAMILY NEGLECT.—Thomas Moore was charged on a warrant with running away from the Borough, leaving his wife anti five children chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Shear •r, who prosecuted on behalf of the Cfnar- dians, said that so far as he could gather the deserti,m had ben brought about by a family quarrel. Prisoner had done nothing to maintain the family for the past eleven week.s. He was a sawyer and could get fairly good wages. At the present time he was earning 24s a week at Manchester. Prisoner's wife and children had been in the Workhouse sines last Thursday. and the wife said she was afraid of him. He had been fined for assaulting his wife.—Bliza Moore. Prisoner's wite, stated that pri-soner was a gcod working man when he k-pt saber, but when he was drunk he caused her and the children to live in dread of him. He hat left them several times.—The case was adjourned for a month to see if a settlement could be effected. NAVAL DE/MITERS —Stephen Pritchard and Patrick O'Btien were charged with being deserters from H.M.S. •'Fnrious" stationed at Chatham since March 23rd.—They were remanded in order that the Naval authorities might be communicated with EXTRAORDINARY CosnuoT.—John Grindley was charged with bring a person apparent y of unsound mind found wan- dering in Bu termarket-street thd morning —P.O. Muskat stated that at 20 minutes to one that morning he saw the prisoner standing on the steps of the Pank in Buttermarket- street, and knocking at the door. He asked him what he wanted and he replied "My old woman's gone in here. I gave her a box of matches to go in" He event-sally came away from the Bank and going to Dr. Peaconke's house, said he lived there. He also said he had "lived in every court in Coventry." Witness brought him to ths Police Station.— Superintendent Monaghan raid he had had a conversation with the man and he seemed ta think that he was in Coven- try yet.—Prisrner was remanded to the Workhouse for 14 days. DISTITBIIANC9 AT 11/F. " MODEL " LODGING HoußE.—John Manraton was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Friars' Green at 4.1- on Friday evening and with committing damaue to five cupboards in the " Model " lodging- /louse to the extent of &I.—P.C. Plumb said be found the prisoner lying on the ground near the door of the lodging' house- He took him to the police station and he was very yiblent.—John Beasley, who lives at the " Model " lodgins- house said the prisoner broke open five cupboards in which food was kept.—A fine of 10s and costs with the alternative of 14 days' imprisonment was imposed. MoNDAY—Before Mr. Birchall (in the chair). Councillor

Smethurst and Mr. S. Wright. THEFT BY A RHYL MAN.—Thorans O'Brien, Rbyl, was aharged with stealing from the outside of the shop of Isaac Houghton. pawnbroker. 28 and 30, Mersey-street, at 6.20 on Saturday :night, a coat and vest value Ifs. Superintendent Monaghan stated that prisoner was seen by a man named Frank Bell loitering about the door of Mr. Houghton's shop. At length he was seen to unhook the coat and vest, and go down Wharf-street. Information was given to Sergeant Bell. who arrested the prisoner in Wharf -street. The bench decided to send prisoner to gaol for a month A DANGEROUS PRICTICE.—A little boy named Albert Roberts was summoned for throwing stones in Lodge-lane on the sth inst.—P.C. (20) Cooper said that he was on duty in Lodge-lane when a girl made a cow plaint to him that the defendant had hit her with a stone. He ultimately saw the defendant who admitted throwing the stone but said he meant to hit ahoy and not the girl. The magistrates fined Zhe defendant 24 6d. INSANITARY PROPERTY.—John Adams. Park-road Newton- le-Willows, was summoned for t-eiug the owner of an insani- tary house in Museum-street.—Inspector Norman said that he received a complaint trom the occupier about the condi- tion of the house number 7, Museum•street, of which the defendant was she owner. lie examined the premises and foun • the back kitchen walls to be damp. The ciefect arose from the want of spouting on the east side of the house and a defective water tub at the back. The yard was also in a de- fective condition.—The magistrates made an order for the necessary work to be done within seven days. defendant to pay the court costs.—Alt.,ert T Moult, 39, Princess-street. Manchester, was summoned in three cases of Insanitary pro- perty.—Orders wet e made for the improvement of the con- dition of the houses —John Smith, of Legh-?treet. was summoned for defects at number 15, Ban —9treet.—lt was stated that the work was in progress and, the case was adjourned for seven days, VAGRANCY.—Patriek Ward, Alfonso Scullen, and Patrick King, 1W-enters. were charged with being rogues and vega- bonds and having been found sleeping in hayricks in Arpley fields On Sunday morning, having no visible means of sub- siatence--P.O tiankey proved the case,ancl said the prisoners were asieep in the hay and he brought them to the polies station.—Rdward Vinch, in the employ of Mr. Hutchinson, said the hay was found pulled about, and on Sundays it was necessary to go to the fields and put it straight, The prisoners had no right whatever where they were found—They were ach tined 5s and costs.

mained in the house until 7.33 and then went to the Unicorn Inn, latching the house do-r. tie stayed in the public house twenty minutes and on guing oat he sew the prisoner leaving his house. Prosecutor immediately went into the kitchen and missed the watch. The matches and cigarettes had been taken from the shop. He follow& the prisoner down Gee-street, and stid to him " Where is that watch ?" and the man replied "It is here I will give it to you and you can say nothing about it." The other articles wers found in the prisoner's pocket. He (the superintendent), asked for a remand for eight days in order that inquiries might be made into his character.—Prisoner was accordingly re- manded. _ .

A VIOLENT WORKHOUSE IxxrATE.—Jane Waterworth, an inmate of the Warrington Workhouse. Is as charged with refusing to perform the task allotted to her on the previous day, also with breaking a pane of glass, doing damage to the amount of is, and with making use of obscene language.— She pleaded guilty.—Mr. Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians, and said that the woman was very troublesome, having bes-n in the Workhouse almost all her life. She had a child four months old. She came into the orkhouse on Saturday evening, having gone out that morn- ng, and was taken to the tramp ward. he was vary dis- irderly, and refused to do any work. She said she wanted ohe police to be sent for, and because they would not send for the police she deliberately smashed a window.—Mrs. Fearn- tide. (the portress) gave evidence, and the prisoner was sent so gaol for a month. Ay OLD OFFENDER.—Margaret Burke who made her 27th appearance was committed to gaol for a month for being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket street at 9.30 on Tuesday night. WIFE Assauty —Joseph Birchall was charged on a war- rant with assaulting Bodelia Eirchall. his wits, on June 9th. —Re was bound over to keep the peace for six months. A TROUBLESOME SOLDIER —INV &LID ED HOM E.—ThOM&S Baguley a soldier, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Horsemarket-street at 11.30 on Tuesday night P.C.'s Sankey and Gilchrist proved the ease.—Prisoner, who has been invalided home from South Africa said that it the magistrates would look over the offence he would cancel his furlough and go back. He could do no good in this town.— Superintendent Monaghan said that prisoner made his 29th I appearance. —Since he had come home on furlough he had been before the Court three times. He had done nothing but drink.—Alderman Francomb t I thought you would have had fighting enough with the Boers without coming trre fighting.—A fine of 54 was imposed.

div.head: County Petty Sessions.
div.p: County Petty Sessions.
WEDNESDAY —Before Messrs J. _!T. Bleckley (in the chair
and J. Ball

BUILDER HEAVILY FlNED.—Albert Payne, the owne• of seven new houses at Sankey Bridges, was summoned tor not providing proper sanitary receptacles as required by the bylaws.—lnspector Kerfoot said that the defendant had been repeatedly warned about the off a ce by letter, and by the Surveyor personally since last February. and he asked the Bench to inflict the full penalty,—Defendant was fined 40s and costs. DRUNK ON LICENSED PREXISES.—Joseph Lawton,of Burton wood. was summoned fcr having been drunk on the licensed premises of William Houghton, " the Chapel House" Buttonwood, on June 30th, and refusing to quit when requested.—William Houghton said that on the 30th nit, the detendant:went into his public-house drunk and was requested toleave. He refused and was put out by his .on.—John Houghton prosecutor's son corroborated. Defendant said he was brought up by Houghton eight years ago for a similar offence and he had never been in the house t ince. This was a bit of spite.—Fined be. MINOR OFFENCES.—The following were fined for drunken- neas.—Bliohael Charles Croft Sc; David Jones Buttonwood, 25 6d; Ralph Hart and Arthur Taylor Buttonwood, 2s 6d each Ellen Hopkins Buttonwood, 2s 6d; Robert Hurst. Sankey, 50 ; James Berry, Buttonwood. 2s 6d.— James Jackson was fined 69, and Thomas Baldwin 2s 6d, for failing to carry lighted lamps on their vehicles at night.

div.head: Runcorn Petty Sessions,
div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions,
AloNniy.—Before Mesers._F. 3, Norman (presiding), and W

Handley. THE STORAGE OF EXPLOSIVF.B.—Mr, William Edgar Lea, ironmonger, applied for and obtained licenses for the storage of explosives at 29 and 12. High-street, Runcorn. Hitherto, the licenses had been granted by the loeal authority A MAINTENANCE ORDER.—Frederick Liwis Bowles, the father of Stanley Bowles. aged 12 years. an in- mate of the Bralwell Reformatory, Sandbach, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute to his son's maintenance during thaikur years he would be confined there.—Superintendent D. earson 'submitted that the boy had been committed to the reformatory on the 30th of last month. Defendant was employed at Wiggs' Works and earned 31s a week He had six other children the eldest of whom was 20 and kept house for him. Defendant had offered a constable Is 6d or 2s a week, and he would ask for 25a week.—Defendant agreed to this, and an order was made accorl ingly. EITEDAND AND WIFE AT VALIANCE —Herbert Johnson, 15 Look-street, was summoned by his wife Margaret, for deser- tion, and complatwant asked for an order under the Married Woman's Summary Jurisdiction Act.—Defendant denied the offence. —The parties declined to come to terms though given an opportunity by the Bench.--Complainant stated the par- ties were married one year and eight months ago, and there were two children of the marriage. The eldest was a year and five months old, and the brby was six weeks old. On the 30th of June she had been turned out of the house, and had the door locked on her. Byldence was given of the de- fendant illtreating his wife whilst under the influ- ence of drink, and of also threatening to murder her.—Sarah Kinsey. a neighbour, corroborated the fact that the complainant was locked out by he: husband.—Defendant stated that he was prepared to take his wife back. "The house was there, and she could come to it if she wished, or go to Dutton Workhouse. Or do what she had a mind." He denied the allegations of the complainant and her witneas, who were only telling "horrible ones" which were untrue The fault lay with his wife's relations, who were always "haggling and picking" at him.—Complainant said that was not so. and only for the kindly interference of her relatives she would have been dead long ago.-1 he Benc't made an order for defendant to pay lie 6d a week towards the maintenance of his wife and two children. MINOR OFFENCES.—PetriGk Connor. 4. Cambridge-street, was fined 51 and 105 6d costs for using obscene langnage.— Lizzie Wheelers. 33. Fryer-street, oh srged with a like offence, was fined 5s and 20s costs, the case having been adjourned from toe previous court.—James Turk. also a profaner, who resided in Cross-street, was fined 514.—Connor paid his fine. but the other defendants went to gaol for the alternative, :even days hard labour.

Liverpool and District Championship.

Sr. HELENS 17. WARRINGTON —This Liverpool and District ChAmpionship match was pia) ed at the St. Helens Corporation Baths on Tuesday night before a large attendance of spectators. Both clubs were strongly represented, and an itteresting game was witnessed. The borne team defended the shallow end during the first half, and had much the best of the game. Robertson, of Warrington, the International goalkeeper, defended in splendid style, but he was beaten by shots from Walker, Mtvity, and Preston, while the visitors failed to score and ends were changed with the score—St He'ens, three goals ; Warrington, none. The play was more even in the second period,and after Walker had again pm red for the home team, Ashton, with a long straight throw, scored the first and only goal for Warrington. Just before the end Mavity pot on another point for S:. Helens, who won by five go Its to one.

SCHOOLBOY DROWNED IN THE WOOLSTON CANAL —A boy named John Wiliam Scholtze, aged 1), of Poulton, was drowned in the canal at %Voolston on Sunday after- noon about three o'clock. Ha and his two brotlit-rs left hQme about 2.30 and went to the bank of the Woo:sten Canal, near the locks. While they were there, some boys whom they did not know Dame up and turned the bridge. D,ceased and another boy jumped on the bridge while it was moving and jumped off again. Deceased again made a jump to get on the bridge, but fell into the water. Hi 3 mates gave an alarm and Mr. John Rathbone, the lock keeper, came up with a lifetitly and threw it to the deceased, who failed to catch it and sank. It was 15 minutes befnre his body was recovered —Mr, Brighouse, county coroner, conducted the inquest on Tuesday afternoon at the Dog and Partridge Inn. when evidence was given hex ring out the above state ment, and the jury re.urned a verdict of" Accidenta deatkr"

The Warrington Hollow Rolling Syndicate. At the Chancery Court of Lancashire, on Monday. before Vice-Chancellor Hall. Mr John Rutherford appeared on behalf of the Hollow Rolling Syndicate of Warrington, to apply for relief under the Act of 1898, owing to the fact that the option to take in cash or shares the payment of a sum of .V 230,000 had not been entered in the contract between the syndicate and Perrins, Limited, the purchasers of their business and patents for the manufacture of metallic tubes. Counsel stated that the company was started in May this year, and was carrying on business most successfully. The only point was that the contract in regard to the option on the part of the syndicate had not been filed, as required by the Act, and a memorandum under the approval of the court was asked for, which ,under a case already decided, would be equal tc the original filing of the coatract.—Mr. Gardner, for the company, concurred in the application, and the memorandum asked for was granted.

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Association Football.

Mr. E. A. Consor has been elected hon, secretary of th- Warrington Association Football Club sod Mr. A. R. Norman hon. treasurer. Mr. T. P. Bradshaw, who was hon. secretary last season, has accepted a position on the cornmitee. Some Ciiappoiatment was occasioned by Mr. Bradshaw's retirement from the position of sects tary, but the new appointments have given much satisfaction. The members of the club are looking for- ward to a successful season.

div.head: Cricket.
div.p: Cricket.

Warrington played off their return fixture with Northern on Saturday on the ground of the Liverpool club at Watezloo. The home team had just returned from a successful tour in Yorkshire and played their strongest side, whilst the visitors la,.:ked the services of E. A. Connor. Mr. .1. W. Bibby was successful in win- ning the toss, and commenced batting with B. Silcock and Thewlis. the start was anything but an auspicious one, for with only seven runs on the score sheet the Rev J. Burrough broke through the professional's defence.

Dr Smith filled the vaczncy, but had only scored three when he touched a riiiog ball into the hands of Henson in the slips, who s?cured it after several attempts. J Callon also had a short stay, an appeal for a catch at the wicket being answered against the batsmar, whilst a good length ball from Hr son acconntcd for G. Clarke tour wickets being down for 20 runs.

J. Briggs joined Silcock who exhibited a sound defence but the new corner soon showed a liking for the old Cambridge bowler's deliveries, and twice in quick suc- C‘23liOn got him away for four. Silcock emulAtf d his pirtner's eximple by placing Henson squire for four,but at 39. Briggs was snapped at the wicket. J. W. Bibby joined Silcock, and a prolonged .itatiti was made, Job eventually relieving Burrough at 50,whilst at 64 Thomp- son took the ball from Henson.

Both batsmen treated the new blwlers with scant respcct, and at 76 Barrough resumed and at °Lee bowled the Warrington e4ptaio. Wll Pacirnore soon began to score rapidly, and his openine essays were a couple of fine drives off each bowler. Runs came at a fair p ,c?, and at 90 Thompson relieved Job.

Podmors sent the 100 up with a drive for two, but the hoisting of this total saw Silcock's patient innings closed Boucher effecting another catch at the wicket. Silcock's innings had occupied a little ov.-r two hours.and his dis- play was one full of merit. Podm ore and J Thompson were now associated both batsmen playing such free cricket that the fielders at once lined the boundary. Henson was called up, but Thompson continued his lively career whilst Poamore by stylish cricket earned repeated cheers.

At 14-7 Job again resurnecl, but the separation was effected oy Henson who bowled Thompson for an invalu- able 29, included in which were six fours. Another use- ful partnership was seen when Hampson joined Pod- more, and at 162 the last-named got his leg in front of one from Henson. Gibqon and Hsmoson gave further trouble, and the total wai taken to 177 before Hampson was caught at cover point.

Northern were left with an hour and twenty minutes in which to save the match, and commenced with the Roy J Burrough and W D Lloyd, Dr. Smith and The wlis being the bowlers. Runs came steadily, despite some brilliant fielding. Lloyd in particular making several fine strokes. It 36 Gibson relieved Dr Smith, and at 44 had the satisfaction of getting Burrough leg before.

Little interest was taken in the remaining cricket, for the match wes practically a draw. A couple of fine catches at the wicket by flampson were responsible for two more wickets and the aggregate at 7.30 had reached 100 for tbe loss of three batsmen. The fielding of the Warringtonians was brilliant.

The second team had Northern 2nd for their oppon- ents the match being played on the Warrington ground. The home captain, winning the toss, took Hawtin with him to the wickets. Both batsmen played very carefully, but at 18 Adamson was beaten by a good ball from Durandu. Houghton quickly scored eight, when be was bowled by Murphy,making room for h Pierpliot. Runs came at a quicker rate with Hawtin and Pierpoint to- gether. Both played attractive cricket, and the score had been taken to 85 before Hawtin was bowled, the outgoing batsman retiring with 31. to his credit.

Duckworth was caught behind the wicket without scoring. Connor joined Pierpoint, but with three tuns added to the score the latter was caught for 31, having played in his usual pretty style. His score including rive tours. The- inning e clos-d for 120.

The score did not appear ro be a large crie,as Northern have 41 very strong batting team and the wicket was in perfect condition, but so well did Crompton and Houghton howl that when time was c all,ed they had lost eight wickets for ',33.

An exciting match was witnessed between St. Paul's and !glands Bros., St. Paul's eventually running out winners by the small majority of four runs. Llwless and Sale each kdocked up eleven for the winners, Butterworth contributing the same number of runs tor 'glands's.
Sankey Wira Mill 3 2nd defeated Earlestown Wesleyans ,2nd by the attbtant!al margin of 38 runs. Hewitt and Clegg batted in fine form tbe-Ir innings realizing 21 and 20 respectively.
Brands' Bros. 2nd gained a victory over Arpley 2nd by 13 runs, Eyre contributing 12 runs to the winners' total of 30.

A HALTON PUBLICAN FINED.
Allegations of Unfairness. How to Conduct a Case.

George Herbert Andrews, of the Village Inn, Halton, was summoned at the instance of the Superintendent of Police for unlawfully permit:it:lg diunkenness up-in his licensed premises on the 24th of June last.
Mr. Fletcher, solicitor, Northwich, appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. A, Browne, silieitor, Warringt )n, tor the defence.

Mr. Fletcher, in opening the case, said on the night in qaestion Police-Constable Upon was oa duty in Halton about half past nine. The Bergeeot who was usually there bad been called away on other buss, so that Upton visited the "Village Inn" alone at half past nine. On going into the Tap Room which was a large room, he found something like 20 Irish labeure:s there most of whom were in a state of intoxication. Four of them he noticed espEcially. They were named King, Grady, Hannon and Dowd. The inmates of the room were all more or less drunk and in a condition they should not have been on a Sunday or any other night, and surely not in a condition that ought to be found in a well regulated public house. Constable Upton drew the attention of the landlord to the condition of the men and told him that he had better not serve them with any more drink. The reply the landlord had given ' (added Mr. Fletcher) was very instructive as illustrating his knowledge of the !icensiog law. He said "I am not going to give them any more because there is no more in." Surely, if the view was, that the landlord of a vil- lage inn was expected to regulate his supply to his CM- towers by that to himself and to go on supplying them until his own was ended, things were getting out of the bounds of proportion. (Laughter.) Notwithstanding the caution given him, the landlord allowed the men present to remain on the premises for about 20 minutes loneer,and then they were all turned out into the streets of Halton in a condition to be described. There was a row and disturbance in the village of such a nature that the Constable followed the four men mentioned and tried to get them home quietly. Michael Dowd, however,was in such a zondition and conducted himself so violently that the Constable had to obtain assistance and lock him up at the Runcorn Police Station, where he was pro- ceeded against and fined the following day. Mr. Fletcher concluded by remarking that it was an undoubted shame that the quet portion of Halton should have been disturbed in that manner, and asked that the person responsible for it should be punished very severely. Police Constable John Upton, stationed at Halton, on oath substantiated his solicitor's statement. He was on duty in the road about 9.30 when his attention was I drawn by seeing a number of Irish labourers going to the urinal outside the" Village Inn." He saw Dowd, King, Grady and Hannon, whom he knew amongst a lot of others. All the men were more or less drunk, but ithree of the four mentioned were drunk. The men went I into the" Village Inn," and he followed. He said to the landlord" Do you know that some of these men, are drunk. You had better net give them any more ?" In , reply the landlord said" They cannot have any more; in fact, I have no more in." Witness then went outside land remained there about 20 minutes when the Irish- men came out ana congregated in the road. He told them they had better get off home," and subsequently they divided, some going towards Rock Savage, and Stockholm, and others towards Sutton. He followed King, Grady, Hannon and Dowd, who were going in the latter direction, because they were creating a great dis- turbance and using very filthy language. Ultimately getting the assistance of some villagers he locked Dowd up as described. On the follow- ing Wednesday the 27th, be called on toe defendant,at which time he had reported the occurrence to his superior officer,and in consequence of instructions told him that he had reported him to the superintendent for permitting drunkenness the previous Sunday night. Mr. Andrews replied very well, I will have to make preparation," Mr. Audrews also asked for the address of:the man Dowd, and witness replied "his present address was Knutsford jail."—Cross examined by Mr. Browne witness adhered to his statement, and denied ever threatening the defendant "that he would do for him." He also repudiated the allegation that he was a friend of the landlord of the" Red Lion S' which was next door to the " Village Inn." Thomas Hortonein the employ of the Ship Canal Com- pany ; Abraham Spruce, labourer, at the Tannery Run- corn and Charles Higgins, labourer, all villagers, residents within 150 yards of the " Village Inn" swore to seeing four Irishmen who were drunk coming from the direction of the "Village Inn." The Irishmen were all drunk and creating a great disturbance. James Allman, labourer, at the Tannery, Runcorn, another resident in Main-street, Halton, swore to being lin bed on the night in question and to getting up to the window to see the cause of a great disturbance. He saw four Irish labourers being followed by Constable Upton. They were very boisterous and the worse for liquor. He could not judge whether they were drunk, however, as he was in the bedroom.

Michael Dowdy farm labourer, employed by Mr. E. Bate, farmer. Sutton. swore to going to the Village Inn on Sunday night the 24th June. at about 7 o'clock and staying there drinking until about quarter to ten. Re was in company with three others, and they were drink- Inc, together. When he went into the" public "he had 24 OAd in his pocket, and when he left be only had the d. (Lauglrer.) He was drunk when he came out of the public-house, but he did not mind (know) what time it wAs exactly. He bad not been drinking anywhere else.

Thomas Barker, landlord of the Red Lion, Halton, said his house was nex door to the "Village Inn" and none of the men had had any of their drink in his house that day.—Cross-examined by Mr. Browne, this witness stated he had come to Court for the purpose of defending his own house and himself. Tnis concluded the prosecution.

-- Mr. Bro wne. for the defence, at the outset submitted that the case had been most unfairly brought forward by the police. He would not attribute it to the Superintendent,the Officer,the Sergeant of Police, or to his friend Mr. Fle,:cher, hut it was unfair that his client did not know that he was going to be proceedel against until three days afterwards. He was never given an opportunity ®f knowing in respect of which man he was going to be proceeded against. It was contrary to the procedure usually taken in 999 cases out Of I,ooo,and be (Mr.Browoe) could only characterise it as unfair and "bitting below the belt." He furrher contended that his client had not permitted drurken- nese ; nor had the evidence of the prosecution shown that he knew that the men were drunk whilst on his premises. All that had ben said was that the men bad had eneugh. And, furthermore, the defendant had no more of the class of beer the Irishmen usually drink This was due to the fact hat durine the week there had been a run of harvee; men at the house, and especially on the previous day. Evidence would b, submitted of the sobriety of the men upon their leaving the house, and as it was an uncontrovertible faet " that the fresh air made a man get worse for drink," no doubt, if the men were affected as described they might have become so whilst travelling the 150 yards, and other etort dis- tances at which the several witnesses for the prosecution had teen them. They were charged with permitting these men to be drunk on the premises, but if they were only discovered to be uriink 150 yards away surely they could not be held responsible. The only case that could be quoted from the Queen's Bench Division was that of a man who had been found drunk in A ditch 20 yards away, and it was held that it was reasonable for the justices to declu e the tact that he had received his drink from the nearest public-house. But that did not apply in this case. In concluding,Mr Browne testified to the good character his client bore. He was an absolute teetotaler, and had conducted his house in a satisfac- tory manner for some years. George Herbert A.udrews said he was landlord of the Village Inn, Halton, and tor 20 years he had been con- nected with the Runcorn Football Club. On the 24th of June he did not see Dowd. or King in his house at all. The Constable did call at the house as stated, but he got the men out in five minutes after the Constable told him. The Irishmen, of whom there woulu be about fifteen, went out of the h 01399 quite soberly, and there was not a bit of a disturbance io front of his house. He saw Constable Upton on thl other side of the road, and a Miss Dale was also standing at the garden gate of bar house opposite. Cross-examined by Mr. Fletcher 7.45 e Irishmen did not enter his house until 10 minutes past eight o'clock. Miss Emily Dale, daughter of Mr. Henry Data, who resided opoosite the " Village Inn," William Ashbrcoke, 44, Norton-street, Runcorn ; Walter Dean, 26,, Norton. street, Runcorn . Albert Williims, a resident two doors off the" Village Inn " ; Mrs Mary Williams, his wife . and Mrs Catherine Dunbavin, Cooke's Cottages, Halton ; all testified to seeing the harvest men after they left the public-house, and at which time they were all perfectly sober. They did not hear any disturbance in the village a?, all.

After a short deliberation, the Chairman said they had decided to convict, but would not endorse the license. Defendant would be fined 203 and costs, £6 108 6d alto- gether. The charges against John King and John Grady, twl of the labourers implicated, were then heard.— King, who appeared, pleaded n-)t guilty, but was fined 54 or seven days..---A warrant was issued tor the appre- hension of GiadF.
Mothers' Trip to Grassendale.

The annual trip in connect-,ion with St. Paul's Mothers' Meeting was held on Monday.when a visit was paid to Grassendale. The party, numbering about 80, started from Kendrick-street in five wag- gonettes, supplied by Mr. II F Greenough, and the drive through the beautiful country was much enjoyed. Arrived at their destination, the mothers paid a visit to the Kerr's celebrated nurseries. After tea and a short ramble a star, was made for home, which was safely reached. There was a concensus of opinion that the outing had been the most suc- cessful on record. The party were accompanied by the Vicar (the Rev I R Tatbuck), Mrs Tarbuck,and Mrs James Richardson.

div.p: THE CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR WORLD'S CONVENTION.

This great gathering of Christian workers from all parts of the world has created widespread attention, and special interest theretore attaches to the article in the July "Quiver "on the subject. It is from the pen of the Rev. F. B. Meyer, B.A. (President of the British National Council) who succinctly describes the origin and purpose of this now almost universal Society—and then forecasts the programme of the coming Convention: —A conspicuous f, awns of the wonderful Christian En- deavour movement is the grand annual Convention. In the United States, between 20,000 and 30,000 Endeav- ourers will gather to their great Feast ot Tabernacles. I use that phrase advisedly, as the Ine..tinffti are held in tents, three of which will hold 9,000 or 10,000 persons each. We have not yet reached such vast figures in Great Britain, though it is expected that the Convention which is being now arranged for July will be attended by at least 30,000 Endeavourers from all parts of the world. . • . All attention and interest are now being concentrated on this great Internatienal Convention, which promises to be unequalled in the laistery of our country as a great international bend, drawing together Great Britain and the United States, our colonies, and all parts of the world into a vast Christian confederation. Before the war broke out our American correspondent told us to expect a contingent of at least ten thousand from across the water ; and even now,not withstanding the increased freights and diminished carrying power, we hope the estimate will not be greatly reduced. And to these must be added tributary streams and conflu- ents from every European country, as well as from Australia, Canada, and all parts of the world. ThA programme of the meetings, from Saturday, July 14th, to Wednesday and Thursday io the following week, is well in band. Its motto is, " The Old Power for the New Age," and the days are crowded with engagements, from the quiet hours and prayer meetings in the morning to the great demonstrations at night. On Monday morning we are to discuss " The Dawning Age and its Problems "—commerical,social and intellectual. In the evening "The Missionary Outlook" is to be our theme. On Tuesday morning a demonstration will be given of World-Wide Endeavour, with testi- monies of the progress and adaptation of the movements in all parts of the world. In the evening addresses will be delivered on " Pente- costal Power." On Wednesday morning "The Messaos of the Churches" will be delivered, by representative men of all denominations ; in the afternoon there will probably be a gigantic Praise Service; and at night Roll Call Services and Closing Words Thursday will probably be devoted to showing our visitors some of the most interesting and beautiful sights of the Metropolis. The place of meeting has been a matter of considerable difficulty. At first it was suggested that we should obtain the use of the largest buildings in London, and have several centres, such as the Queen's and Exeter Halls, the City Temple, and the Metropolitan Tabernacle. But the immense difficulty of locomotion for so many thousands of visitors, the time and expense involved, and the ,perplexity of directing strangers, negatived this proposal as not the best, it some more practicable method could possibly be devised. Wembley Park was suggested ; then our attention was turned to the Alexandra Palace, situated on a command- ing site in the north of London, and surrounded by extensive and beautiful grounds. It has tad rather a chequered career, but not because of any deficiency in the structure itself, or in the conveniences it affords for the reception of large masses of people. Its main auditorium will seat about 10,000 persons and there are other spacious halls which will contain some thousands. The arrangements for catering for vast crowds are perfect. We can turn the banqueting hall into a vast dormitory for ladies, and there will be ample space for pitching the camps for the accommodation of young men, as well as (perhaps) the American tent with its capacity for 9,000 persons. In many respects the Alexandra Palace will be preferable to Wembley Park, because it will give greater security against inclement weather. It might have exposed us to a great deal of inconvenience if we had been under canvas amid drench- ing rain, such as sometimes falls to our share even in July. And though the Palace may not possess quite so much of the picturesque and al fresco, it will certainly be more secure against the fickleness of our climate. . . . The list of speakers and preachers will include D. r and Mrs. Clark, the Rev. C. M Sheldon, the author of" What Would Jesus do ? ' and Mr. Baer, who. with many other prominent men, have definitely promised to be with us from the United States ; whilst familiar and honoured leaders, like Dr. Handley Moule, Dr. Monro Gibson, and the Revs. J. H. Jo wett and A. Connell will contribute of their best ; the ladies beine ably represen- ted by Lady Henry Somerset and Miss Marianne Farn- ingham.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
CHINA.

The, Attack upon Tientsin. Capture of 62 Guns. BERLIN, WEDNESDAY. A despatch dated the 1413 inst. states that on that day the whole of the Chinese position, includ- ing the walled town and the citadel, was captured, and 82 guns fell into the hands of the allies. Details are not yet to hand. In another despatch, dated Taku, July /6:b, the officer in com- mand of the German squadron says regulir railway communication between Taku and Tien- tsin will be opened on the 1812. It was decided to day that the senior officer of the station should have military control of the line, until the situation should make it possible to hand it over to the ordin- ary railway au`horities. The British Admiral wished that it should be banded over at once. The Russians prepared the line, and now occupy it.—Reuter.

• Startling Story from Shanghai. Russia Secretly Negotiating with Prince Tuan. Li Hung Chang Conniving. The •• Globe' correspindent at Shanghai telegraphs :—llusaia has recently been secretly negotiating with Prince Tuan's Government, Li Hung Chan 7. conviving. The viceroy Liu Bun Yi has actually received details from Tuan, but failed to apprise the Powers. Certain high authorities in , the Yangtze province favour a secret alliance with Russia. Chan (.3i4i Tung, however, dissents.

, Investigttions 0 Paardeberg, the scene of Cronje's last stand, show that large quantities of ammunition, riflNs, and sh4lE., were buried with dead Boers and elsewhere. The Australian Bushmen • have proved extremely clever in discovering these strange graves. Thl undamaged weapons and ammunition have been removed to prevent their future use.
British Consul at Beira Fatally Stabbed.
LOURENCO MARQUES, TUESDAY, JULY 17. Mr. .1E Nlactnasters, British Consul at Boira. WIS fatally stabbed yesterday when on duty up country. Ms assailant is said to be an American.

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

Captain Ferrer, late of the South Lancashire Regiment. who has for several weeks past been do- ing duty with the Ist Battalion Royal Lancashire Reserve Regiment, has in consequence of ill-health been compelled to relinquish hie employment with the Royal geeerves. Captain Dudgeon who lately gaveup the appoint- =ent of adjutant of the ad Battalion South Lan- I cashire Regiment, has been appointed to the staff in readia and has taken over the appointment of deputy assi4ant adjutant general at Nerbudda, Bengal. Captain Dudgeon, wko has been nearly 15 years an offic,r of the South Lancashire Regiment, has passed the staff college course but has not pre- viously served on the staff. Major F. Lamb, Ist Battalion South Lancashire Regiment who was wounded in the fighting in Natal when Colonel McCarthy O'Leary was killed returned home from South Africa several weeks ago and has so far recovered as to be able to take part in the Bisley rifle meeting wnere as usual this accomplished marksman has again been very successful. When he rejeine his regiment he will take over the appointment, of second in command of the Ist battalion, which position has been vacant since Lieutenant Colonel tall was proasoted to his present rank to command the battalion in succession to the late Lieutenant Colonel McCarthy O'Leary. A North Western District Company Militia Medical Stiff corps is now being formed and recruiting is to be carried out for the company in the Bth and 40th Regimental districts at Warring- ton and also in the 22nd (Cheshire) Regimental district. Second Lieutenant Evans, of the tP,h Battalion Cheshire Regiment, has been appointed to a com- mission in the reeular service, becoming Second Lieutenant in the 2ad Battalion Manchester Regi- ment in South Africa. where Mr. Evans has been serving with the old 2ad Cheshire Militia which he joined in May of last year. Lieutenant Chaffery, sth battalion Liverpool Regiment, with headquarters at Warringten has gone to South Africa for service with the Ist bat- talion Liverpool Regiment while Second Lieutenant, 14yrne just appoint e Ito the sth battalion has joined that corps iu Ireland. According to the official list of trainings issued by the War Office the 9th Yeomanry Brigade which consists of the Cheshire Yeomanry and the Lanca- shire Hussar, was timed to commence training in brigade camp at Altcar on Tuesday and the training will terminate on 1s of next month. Colonel Lord Gerard, Lancashire Hussars, commands this brigade.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

SUNDAY EVENING SERVICES IJ,UILL CLIFF GRAVEYARD. sarvices are being continued and are attended increasin: congregations. Last Sunday night there was one of the largest congregations this season. The Pastor, the Rev J. S., Hughes, conducted the wlnle ser- vice preaching from the words " Arise, go into the plain cud I will talk with thee there," Ezekiel 111, 22. The cengregation followed him with great attention. The evening was an ideal one for such a service.warm,bright mud clear and the surroundings were really delightful. Tho singing on Sunday night was not up to the mark 6.nd would be gr, atly improved if the people crowded nearer the preacher but nevertheless the singing and the preacher's voice could be distinctly heard in Stoc4ton Heath. The subject riven for next Sunday evening is 0 is life worth Living ?"

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
RESIGNATION OF THE REV. F. E. MILLER, EARLESTOWN.

We understand that the Rev F E Miller's connec- tion with the Baptist Church, Earlestown. will ter- minate in the course of a month or so, after six years ministration. Mr Miller came to Earlestown from Red ruth, and the severance of his connection with the church will no doubt be smatter of regret to the congregation. EA.RLESTOWN TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION CLASSES.

The following results of the examinations in physiography and mathematics held in connection with the above classea,have came to hand. —Phycio- graphy: J C Rawlings,A Ist class ;Ethel E Bateman, Gertrude Knowles, A I2nd class; Edith Bunting, Theo Clare, It A Robinson, E Ist class ; John Claw- thorns, Annie Benny, E D Lyons, E 2nd class.— Mathematics: Benry Ecldington, Stage 111, 2ad class; Giles Collings, Stage 11, 2nd class; Thomas Benison and Theo Clare, Stage 1, 2nd class. POLICE CASES.

At the Newton Police Court on Tuesday morn- ing before Mr.Gillespie.Richard Turner was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap and was fined 2s 6d and costs.—Thomas and Annie Finingan of no fixed abode were charged with being drunk in Earlestown the previous night, and were each sent to goal for seven days.— Michael McDermott, Legh-street, Earlestown for a similar off ancelwas finad3.

EARIESTOWN WELSH CONGREGATIONALISTS. A picnic in connection with the above took place on Saturday afternoon to Frodsham. About 40 jour- neyed in a large wagonette, leaving Earl.,.stown about one o'clock and after a pleasant drive reached Frodsham about half past three. Half an hour later tea was served at Mersey View, and the remainder of the time was spent in rambles about the hills. The drive home was very eojoyable, Earlestown , being reached about 10-30. CHRISTIAN BRETHREN'S SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The annual treat and field day of the children attending the above school took place on Saturday afternoon under very favourable circumstances. They walked in procession from the school, a van ! conveying about 30 of the younger children to a field adjoining New Bradley Farm, Burtonwood, kindly lent by Mr. Kilshall, where games of vari- ous kinds were indulged in. Tea was served in the field, and afterwards, until nine o'clock, the youngsters thoroughly enjoyed themselves. THE HAYDOCK ZXPLOSION.—ANOTHER DE A.TH; John Fitzpatrick, of Heath-road, Ashton in- Ntakerfield, one of the ten men who were terribly injured by an explosion of gas at the old Boston Pit, Haydock, over a fortnight ago, succumbed to his injuries last week-end. This is the seventh man of the ten who has died. —Mr. S. Brighowe, county coroner, formally opened the inquest on Fitzpatrick on Monday night, at the Waggon and Horses Inn Mr. A. Ellis, solicitor, of Wigan, and Mr. John Robinson, general manager, represented the com- pany. After evidence of identification had been given, the inquest was adjourned till the 21st Aigust. BAPTIST YOUNG PEOPLE'S SOCIETY OF CHRISTI ILN
ENDEAVOUR.

The members of this society, to the number of 18 had a picnic on Saturday to Chester. Leaving Earlestown by the 845 a.m. train, they reached the city about 11 o'clock. After a ramble round the walls they partook of dinner, and afterwards sailed up the river by barge as far as Eccleston Ferry where they landed and walked to Eaton Hall. After viewing the conservatory they made their way to Eccleston Ferry, where tea was partaken of. The return journey to Chester by barge in the evening was very pleasant and was much enjoyed. Newton was reached about 10 o'clock, after a mo 9:, pleasurable outing. CHARGE OF STEALING A GIG.

At Liverpool County Quarter Sessions, on Tues- day, John Broderick (39), labourer, pleaded not guilty to a charge of stealing a gig at Newton-le- Willows belonging to Jacob Winter. Mr. Ilarrison prosecuted, and prisoner was defended by Mr.Rigby Swift. Winter purchased the gig for £3 53, and afterwards left it outside a public-house while he and some companions had some drink. The trap was missed from the door, and the prisoner woo worked on a neighbouring farm, was afterwards found to have sold it to a greengrocer for £3 10s.— Broderick, who was given an excellent character, stated on oath that be met a man unknown drawing the gig along the road.and he purchased itithinking he could "make a bit" on the transaction.—lie was found not guilty, and was dischargad. ALLEGED THEFT OF A BUILDER'S HOD.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, John Vincent, was charged with steal- ing a hod, valued at 2s 6d, the property of Samuel Findley, from buildings in course of erection, in Wargrave-road, Newton, on July 14th. He plealed not guilty.—Prosecutor said the defendant was employed by hiin on July 3rd and he paid him off on July 14th at 11 a.m. When he paid him off, de- fendant asked him for the hod, and he said he could not have it because it wacs his (prosecutor's) pro- perty. However, defendant took it. He followed him and gave him in charge of the police.—Defen- dant said the hod was left on the buildings by a man who had gone away. It was then broken, and could not be used. He asked the prosecutor if he could mend it, and he was allowed to do so. It was not the property of the prosecutor.—The Magistrates' Clerk said the hod was not Pinaley's property.—The case was dismissed and defendant was allowed to keep the hod. GOOD TEMPLADS.

The Hope of garlestown Lodge meeting was held in Wargrave-road Hall on Monday evening. Bro. Cutler CT presiding. Sister Owen reported visiting several sick members who were progressing favour- ably. Bro. Newman reported that the picnic had been a pleasant one, all having thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Sisters Ord and Newman were ap- pointed to receive and arrange the flowers and Sister Woods to arrange a programme for the thwer service. Bro. Newman announced the arrangements for tne juvenile treat. Bro. Litherland. (Star of the East Lodge) Warrington. addressed the Lodge, tendering the greetings of the Lodge, which were accepted. The programme was " Letter Night," Bro. Newman responsible, and letters were road from Bro. Nixon, D.S.J.T. Warwickshire,Sister Houghton (Hope of Bolton), Lance Corporal Heyes, Kimberley, also the experience of Bra. Spong on Spion Kop where be was wounded and taken prisoner by the Boers. Though Riven up by the doctors, as the bullet had entered the hip and come out at his shoulder traversing both lungs, he had recovered and was invalided home. Letters were also read from Bros Proctor,SAychelle,and a Brother in Calcutta and from one in Jerusalem. PRESENTATION TO Mn. DAVID WILLIAMS, EARLESTOWN.
On Saturday evening there was .an „impprtan

gathering of Trades' Unionists, of the Newton-in- Makerfield district in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown' for the purpose of making a presenta- tion to Mr. David Williams, who tor over .`.30 years was a trusted official of the Amalgamated -,tociety of Engineers. The presentation took the form of' a purse containing £4O, and the award of merit known as " The Victoria Cross" of the A.S.E. In addition Mrs. Williams was presented with an electro. tea pot, suitably engraved, and Alias Williams with a hand mirror, brush and comb. For over 20 years Mr. Williams was employed at the London and North Western Company's Wagon Works at Earlestown, but he resigned the position ' some few months ago. Prior to the presentation ! tea was provided for the subscribers, and the sub- sequent meeting was presided over by Mr F H Rose of Liverpool. The presentation was made by Mr G H Barnes, general secretary of the A.S.E.—Mr. S. ! Woods, M.P., who should have presided, sent a handsome subscription with the following letter of apology ;—" I have been away on the Continent ! and other places, and I regret exceedingly that I shall not be able to be with you at the presentation on Saturday. Had I been able I should have been only too pleased to have been there, and to have testified to the good work Mr. Williams has done. I trust you will have a successful gathering with hest wishes for his further success."— I am yours faith- fully, S. WOODS.—Mr. Williams very suitably replied to the presentation, and in the course of his re- marks alluded to the position of the society with which he was connected.
Chilian Government and a Warrington Firm.

On Tuesday morning the firm of Messrs, W A Bishop and Co., borax manufacturers, Warrington, received the following cablegram from the British Vice-Consul at Arica, Chili, South America : " Has granted permission; time to commence two months; time to terminate two years.' This cablegram ' refers to the concession from the President of Chili to the laying down of a mono-rail from Chilcava to Arica by the company, which will open out inex- haustible supplies of borate of lime, which can be placed on the Liverpool markets at an exception- ally cheap rate.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

CANAL MYSTERY. About half past five o'clock on Siturday morninl. John Mitchell, a collier, of 199, Merton B toll-road, St Helens, when passing along the canal side neir the bottom of Park-road, found the body of a newly-born child in the water. Constable Whalley was called, and removed it to the mortuary. Toe child had topen in the water a considerable time, and was fully developed. tut much decomposed. At St. Helens Town Hall. on Mora day night, Mr. S Brighouse, county coroner, held the inquest on the body of the child.—Police-Constable Whalley said that on the information of John Mitchell he went to the canal, and removed the body, which was much decomposed, to the mortuary.—Dr. Casworth said that as the result of his post-mortem he formed the opinion that the child had no separate existence from the mother.—A verdict ot " Stillborn " was returned. YEOMANRY CHURCH PARADE. The first annual church parade of B Troop of the Lan- cashire Hussars was held on Sunday afternoon at Helens Parish Church. The troop, numbering 95, ;assembled at the Town Hall at two o'clock, under Major ' W. Lee Palkinc,ton, who w,.s accompanied by Lieutenant Leonard Pilitin,gton, of Lytham. Tney were here joined by Bandmaster Batley and twenty-three members of the band. During the past twelve months the troop has made a great advance, and notwithstanding that over thirty members attached themselves to the 32nd com- pany of the Imperial Yeomanry in South Africa, the troop is at its full strength, close on fifty recruits having joined. The Parish Church was filled by a very large congregation, and the Rev. Canon Willin's,who conduc- ted the servic., made a syinpathetic reference to the death of Lieutenant T. Douglas Pilkington, of the Royal Dragoons, who was Idled at Nitral's Nek. Several of the hymns were accompanied by the band, and Canon Willink preached a stirring and interesting sermon from the text " Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." Twenty members of the troop took part in the service at Holy Cross Catholic Church, which was conducted by Father Collins. The band subsequently rendered a splendid pro- gramme of music at the Vitoria Park, where a cilec- tion was made for the Mayor's war fund.

DISGRACEFUL SUNDAY SCENES. At St. Helens on Monclay,Ed ward and Thomas Leahey two brothers, of Canal Bank, and two well-know char acters, were summoned for assaulting Inspector St'..el and Police Constable Harrisen on Sunday. Edward wal also charged with being drunk and disorderly. Edward pleaded guilty, and Thomas not guilty.—lmpector Steel said that about ten minutes past ten on Sunday night he found Edward drunk and disorderly lu Rtven-street Be was almost oak .d and was shouting and chaliengirQ to fight everyone who passed along the street. He advised him to go away, and afterwards went for assistance. Be and Police Constable Harrison then went, upon which Edwards ran at the constable and butted him over. Tnev got him on the ground after a fierce struggle, and when they were putting on the handcuffs Thomas ran out from rhe crowd and kicked them. They , were very severely handled, and on making a secone attempt to handcuff Edward several of the crowd assisted Thomas to beat them. The in ipector got a lblack eye, and had his left arm disabled —Chief-Con- s-able Wood gave formal evidence that Edward Leahec was within two years—in September last—convicted of ass 'tilting two constables. Edward hid been convicted thb ty-nine times and Thomas thirty-six times, the latter havieg served twelve mouths for unlawful wounding The bench imposed the maximum penalty on one charge.—Edward going to gaol for nine months' hard a bour, and Tnomas for six months. FATAL TRAP ACCIDENT. Mr. S. Brighouie, county coroner, held the inquest on Saturday mornine, at the Engine Inn, Parr. St. Helens, on the body of Edith Chisnall aged two years and fou• months, daughter of a collier, of Derbyshire Hill, wh,, was killed on Thursday by being run over by a trap,— Mrs. Chisnall said the child was in the roadway helpinc its grandfather to carry coals in, when the accident occurred. The child died about an hour after, eipe Snufilebottom a neighbour, said that as the trap wee close up to the child it started to go across the road. Th. horse knocked it down, and the wheel went on to it. The driver jumped out and picked up tee Franc is Rowley said she saw the accident, and did not think the driver could prevent R.—Patrick Corry, aced seventeen, of 18. Princess-street. Wigan, driver for Messrs. Christopher Bros tea merchants, said be had been driving about three years. When going aloeg Derbyshire Hill-road at a very moderate pace he saw the child stan ling by the side of the road. When he wa. about four or five yards away it started to run. Ile pulled up, but could not keep the horse off the child. He backed toe wheel off the child's ho ly, and gave it to the grandfather. He followed into the house, and told the mother to send bra doctor at once. The doctor did no come while be was there. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and exonerated the driver from blame.

div.head: NEWTON s rAt3BING CASE.
div.p: THE NEWTON s rAt3BING CASE.
Prisoner Committed for Trial.

Michael Mannion, a collier, living at Hayd3ck was charged at the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday with unlawfully and maliciously wounding one Patrick Delaney at Newton on June 4cla (Whit Monday), with intent to do him some grevous bodily harm. The pro-e3utor, who is also a collier, said he lived at 76, Lyme Street, Haydock. On the night in question he went to the Swan lon, Newton Common, about nine o'clock. Patrick Moran, Michael Mannion and Patrick McFarlane went with Lim. They each had a drink and left about ten o'clock and started on their way home. The prisoner and himself "had some words" and then came to blows. He hit Mannion, who fell and got up again directly, and then witness got hold of him and threw him down by the hedge. Just than Walter Duncan and Ernest Parsons came up, and prisoner and himself separated. Witness went away with Parsons about seven yards, and he asked one of the men to bring his cap. Whilst waiting for it the prisoner came up behind Parsons and made a sudden rush at him (prosecutt.r) end stabbed him. He ran away about 20 yards and then he stood an I said to the prisoner. "You have stabbed me and ruined me," while to the "boys" he said "Don't go away." Parsons came up to him and witness hardly knew what he was doing. Ha could not see. He was dazed, but he did not fail. Blold was ft-ming from the wound. flu companions wanted to take him to the Cottage Hospital at Haydock, but he refused to go. Two other men came no at the time and walked part of the way home with him, but he did not know who they were. When h,- ,2ot home two policemen came to see him as well as Dr Henderson. The newt day witness went into the hospital and staye I there u ti that morning, the 16t Mkt. The Pole in his trousers was where the knife went through them. He did not know what he was stabbed with.

Patrick Moran and Walter Duncan gave evidence. Dr. Henderson said that at one o'clock on the morn- ing of the sth Jane he was called to 76, LctriP-sroet, Hayclock, to see toe pro4ecutor. whom he found lying on the floor suffering from a wound in the abdomen. It was an inch and a varter deep and half an inch long, and it h,cl been bleeding considerably. The wound Wa9 a clean cut, sue 'i as might have been produced by a knife or some other sharp instrument. He dr ssed the wound and had the man put to bed. He saw him the following morning and nerivaded him to go into the Has dock Cottags Hospital, and he had attended him from that time to the pre3ent. Be considered the w und a dangerous on,,partly from its rxtent and partly from its po-ation. The wound had since healed, and the prosecutor was now out of danger. Serge int Lings said he apprehended the prisoner at six o'clock on the morning of the sth June at Haydock and charged him with unlawfully wounding Delaney with into :t to do him grievous bodily harm by stabbing him id the lower part of the body with a knife or some Wher sharp instrument, and his reply was" Not guilty of stal)bing. I had no knife anywhere." Prisoner was committed to e.h. Aiz.s for trial.

At a meeting or tills coca.nictt.e the preliminary plan for a new laualry was su omitted and approved, and Messrs. 0 ven were r- qa -s1 to prepare detailed draw- ings and approximate estimates of cost for submission to the Bo trd. It was recommeaded tnat the Clerk b- directed to iastruet tin various relieving officers con- cerned to report to the gouge Committee as speedily possinle all cis‘s of persona becoming chargeable by reasoa of suffering fro n delirium tremens, and that no proceedings wider the Vagrant Act be taken in any such ca e until directions thereon have been given either by the committeA or the Board. At another meeting the relienation of Mr. and Mrs. Cliff ord was accepted, while at a nreting on tae 13ta July the master was instructed t !advertise for a male attendant and a general servant— man and wife—for the new infirmary oa cite same terms as before. It was recommended ,loa,t Mrs Griffin, assistant to the matron, have a gratuity of £lO granted her upon her leaving the Guardians, she not re-ing en titled to benefit under the Superannuation Act 1896. Mr. HICKMAN moved, and tin It >v. \V. H. DRUMMOND seconded, tne adoption of the minutes. Mr. CLA.REE asked on what acco-nt tho payment n £lO to Mrs. Griffin was rec marnendeu. At this point the CLERIC read a letter from Mrs. Griffi, as follows :—" Will you pardon me far taking th, liberty of writing to ask if you will kindly consider my , case with a view to grantina me some campeosation on my leaving your service to enable me to start life again. You will be aware that when the Superannuatio i Act was passed I was requested by the Guardians to contrac out of the same. Having done so I have now nothing to fall back upon, and having served you for the past five years, and being entirely without means, may I be that you will be so kind as to entertain my application May I also ask you if you will kindly grant ins a testi- monial." _ _ .
Mr KgOV7LES : What wages does Mrs. Griffin receive

The CHAIR3VIN : Twenty-live pounds and rAtio,is. Mr. KNOWLES said the members of the Board wer, not brouht there for charitable purposes. They went t serve the interests of the ratepayers, and they would be guilty of a breach of duty to toe ratepayers if they granted the sum of £lO. If they passed the minutes as trit'y stood they would simply be making Mrs Griffin pr sent ot £lO. Legally they had a right to do so, hut mo ally hey had no right to make presents out of the po kets of the ratepayers. He moved as an ameniment that the £lO be not granted. Mr. PILLING seconded.—He said that Mrs. Griffin was an elderly person when she came into the service of the Board, and was really takeh on more out of charity than anything else. He had no douht that if the apoointme t had been left open she would not have had the aligi to chance of election. Mr- ASHCROFT said he did not think the ratepayers' money should be thrown away in the manner proposed by the committee. Mrs. Griffin's length of service was oely 4 years. Mr. CLARICE suporrtei the amendment. r Mr, DAVIES said that Mrs. Griffin was taken into the seivica of the Board through the appeal of Mrs. Ward on her behalf. She ought to have saved enough money, which would now have been of the greatest assistance to her.

The Rev. W. H. DRUMMOND Said he did not think tna matter had been looked upon in its true asp .ct. Mrs Griffin had been in service under the Poor Law for 40 years which was a long period, and to mak.3 her a small grant on leaving was only fair. There was a certain amount of responsibility on the Board not to eas-, tier away entirely without any compensation. They had practically forced Mrs Griffin ti contract out of the Superannuation Act, for she was told that she would have to go if she did not do so. The CHAIRMAN said he wished to lay before the Board o re or two facts. It was said that Mrs. Griffin had been taken into the service of the Board as an act of charity. That was not so. She was taken on as an act of busi- ness. It was thought that as she had had 40 years' experience and had been matron of a large workhouse that envecgernent would be a wise one. He did not tiesita.te to ay that for the first two years she did some I extremely good and valuable work in assisting to carry out the reforms that were initiated during that time in the way of increasing the discipline of the House and getciao rid of abie-nodied men and women who were -ponYing on too ratepayers. At the 'present time they had no able-bodied inmates of the workhouse It seemed unfair that a woman grown old in :he service of the Poor Law shauld be sent away without any recompense whatever. Mr. tlicE.m.ktsi slid it was understood when Mre.Griffin was debarred from receiving the benefit of the Super- annuation Ac 5 coat she would be entitled to some com- pensation when leaving. Mr. A. JOLLEY : NO, no. Mr. PILLING Nonsense. The acci-ndinent was then put. Nine voted for it,and the Chairman declared it lost, Mr. PILLING moved that Mrs Griffin be paid the sum of £5. Mr. MALKIN seconded, but this amendment was also lost. Mr. HouhuroN moved, and Mr. A. JOLLEY seconded, that the matter be referred back to the House Committee, and this mati in was agreed to. The remaining portion of the n mutes was apnroved. There was no other business of publie interest.

div.head: WARRINGTON DISTRICT NURSING
div.p: WARRINGTON DISTRICT NURSING
ASSOCIATION.
The New Nurses' Horne.

It is just three rays since the District Nursing Aso dation started work in our midst, and it is gratifyii.g to note the steady progress which has been made in that time. Oat of very small beginnings the Association b3s• grown until it his b 'come one of our recognised institu tions, and its work is known and valued by all. Not the least important of her many gracious mani festations of intereat in her p,opie,is the formation by our much loved Queen, of an Inst:tution for the supply of trained nurses for the help and c irnfort of the sick Door in their own 110(130S, and to thi4 Institution which bears her name the local association is affiliated. As year by yoar, the demand for the services of the Nurses has increased the staff has had to be proportion- ately increased, until it now consists of a superintendent and four nurses, and arrangements will be made for an additional nurse as so.on as a suitable one can be found. The accommodation in the original borne. at 41, Arpley street, has for some time be found to be inadequate,and the Committee has cause to congratulate itself on havii24 secured, on a five years' lease,the very suitab'e premises 21. Arpley-street, into which the nurses moved a month azo. The new Home consiss of two complete hcams with two communicating doors, one on the ground floor and another on the first floor. Ou the ground floor, besides the Superintendent's sitting room, Nurses' sitting room, dining room, box room, and kitchen, is the " District Room," a luxury highly appreciated by the nurses. In it are pegs for cloaks and bonnets, a rack for boots and slippers, rails for drying wet cloaks (for the nurses are out in all weather, and it is not always summer), cupboards for ointmen's, lotions, etc., for appliances, and for clothing given for the use of the patients. Here, also, is a deep porcelain sink, fitted with hot and cold water, in which appliances which have been lent out can be cleansed and disinfected on their being returned. In the small yard attached is accommodation for housing and cleaning the bicycles, those now indi pensable items of a District Nurse's ourfit. Each nurse rejoices in the possession of her own bedroom (of which there are eight) a poliseasion always dearly pr,zed by those whose lives are lived" in public." There are also two bathrooms. A considerable sum Of money has been expended on renovation
adaptation, and, most important rf all,on the thorou

_ ow-A.-hauling of the sanitary arrangements, substituting ails, which might be antiquated or defective, for such as are acknowledged to be hygienic and safe. Increased accommodation brings increased expencli• tore, and the funds of the Association will now be taxed to twit utmost limit. To extend this limit,to help on the vvirk, and to encourage the nurses in their arcluous and often depressing labours among the sick poor of War- ringtm, contribution large or swab wilt be gratefully received by the Superintendent at the Horne, or by the TrLasurer, F. Monks, Esq., Walton Old Hall.

div.head: SERIOUS FIRE FIRE AT COCKHEDGE MILLS.
div.p: SERIOUS FIRE FIRE AT COCKHEDGE MILLS.
Exciting Scenes.

There was great excitement in the town at 9.40 on Wednesday morning, when the" bezzer "at Cockhedge Mills sounded loud and long. Of late I the Wowing of this buzzer has denoted the reception I of important news from the seat of war, so that on Wednesday people thought first of Nialeking and La lysmith and men were at a loss to know what it I meant. The clanging of the fire bell, however, was heard a few minutes lacer, and hundreds of people were soon hurrying to the mill. It was found that a ft's was raging in the spinning room on the third storey,friction at the headstock of one of the mules having caused a spark to ignite the cotton. The flames spread with great rapidity and as may be readily imagined, the fifty or sixty females who were at work in the room above were seized with panic. Toe staircase was blocked and a rush was at once made to the emergency, escape which has been erected on the outside of the building. The terrified girls who were enveloped in em )ke,in some cases, threw themselves from one ladder te ( he next,the height of a storey. The ladders were s imetimes completely blocked and had it not been for the plucky conduct of PC. Steuart and a couple of workmen some of the girls might eave been seriously injured. It was a most excit- ing time, and wken the girls descended one by one ro the bottom rung of the ladder they had to leap the remaining distance, being caught by policemen Ind others standing below prepared to receive ( hem. Stuart ana a workman subsequently searched the top storey for any who might not have escaped ,eit, they found that all had got away. Meanwhile the alarm had spread all over the building and the whole of the employees made a rush for the mill yard. Toe fire brigade, under the direction of Superin- tendent Turner were soon on the scene with the steam engines "Captain "and " Majer," and a fire elcape. plentiful supply of water was obtained from the reservoir at the back of the mill, and the tire engines asAsred by tee powerful eugines be- longing to the firm were quickly at work. One of the Corporation engines worked from the mains and the ocher the " Captain " was stationed near the bank of the reservoir. The latter, after working a few minutes broke down for some unexplained reason and was of no further use. An alarming incident occurred during the coupling of some reels leer the reservoir. Police-constable Carter and two firemen were walking over the reservoir, when suddenly the plank broke, and the three men were precipitated into the water. Fortunately they sac- :eeded in escaping with a " ducking " more wel- come than otherwise in the prevailing heat. The fire brigade were greatly assisted by the mill employees and before long the fire was under con- trol. Toe floors and ceilings of the rooms are if

Iron and concrete and thii—prevented the flames from spreading to any other part of the building. ' kieeat, damage, was, however. caused by the water which poured like rain upon the rooms beneath, in mhici, were a large number of valuable carding machines and a quantity of cotton. At 11-10 the fire was extinguished but it was found that in the spinning room the machinery was in many cases h,qond all recovery, owing to fire and water, and a large portion of the boarded floor was also burnt to charcoal. The whole of the cotton stuff had either been burned, or so soaked with water as to be use- Less. Every credit is due tG the firemen and their ss istan ts for the admirable manner in which they carried out their work under tryiag conditions. But for their untiring energy the fire would no doubt, cave been much more serious. As it is the damage is estimated at several thousand pounds, but it is covered by insurance.

Sturgeon Caught in the Mersey. A remarkably tine sturgeon was caught in the Mersey at Fiddler's Ferry on Saturday. A couple of young men who were boating saw the fish in shallow water. One of them went in and secured it with a rope, and with some difficulty it was dragged into the boat. The fish weighed about ten stone and was nearly six f.et in length, Volunteer Intelligence. The list just issued of officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the Volunteer force who have been awarded the Volunteer long service medal, contains the fohowing names of members in the Warrington Volunteer Battalion, namely, Sergeants 5.3, H. impson and T. A. Ward.

L. 84N -W. Railway Company and St. Helens Traders.—Garston Dock Scheme Abandoned. A Lords' Committee on Weduesd•iy concluded the consideration of the London and North-Western Railway Bill, which, among other things,empowered the company to construct a new dock at Garston. The Chairman (Lord Brougham) announced that the Committee found the preamble of the bill proved, subject to the condition that if the new dock were constructed the preferential rates which were granted to the St. Helens traders in respect of the existing docks would be extended to the new dock. —Mr Page, Q.C., on behalf of the promoters, announced that,in view of the Committee's decision they would withdraw the dock clauses from the bill.—Mr. Wedderburn asked that the company should be ordered to pay the opponents' cots, but the Committee refused the application. Funeral of the late Mrs. Warrington Wood The remains of the late Mrs. Ann Lilies Warring- ton Wood, who died at Edgar House, Bath, on Wed- nesday morning, were interred in the Warrington Cemetery on Saturday morning. The deceased lady, who was 72 years of age, was the widow of the late Mr John Warrington Wood,the famous Warrington sculptor, who died in December, 1886, and she had resided at Bath for some time past. The funeral was of a very quiet character. The principal mourners w-,re :—Mr and Mrs Fleming Hamilton, the Misses Maud and Blanche Hamilton, Mr Char!es Ell Leith Flay, Mrs Darbyshire, Mr J W Darby- shire, Miss Bailey, and Miss A Jenkins. The Rev. Canon Willis officiated. The coffin was of polished , oak with brass mountings. The funeral arrange- ment s were carried out by Messrs F Ealand and Co., of Bath.

Confirmation at the Parish Church. A coofirmation service was conducted at the Parish Church on Saturday afternoon by the Right Rev. Dr. Chavasse, Bishop of Liverpool. Seventy- five candidates were presented, the numbers from the various churches being :—Sc, Paul's, 10 males. 6 females ; St. Barnabas', 8 males, 14 females ; St. margaret's,Antield, 2 males; Parish Church, 2 males 6 females; Holy Trinity, 6 males, 21 females. The el Jrgy who attended included the Rector (Rev CP non Willis), Revs Canon Penryhn, E C E Cs.rlton, i R Tarbuck, L W Thomas, J H G Hollingworth, G W Dickenson and A S Cameron. There was a large congregation. Before and after the ceremony of laying on of hands, the Bishop ' delivered helpful addresses to the candidates. He said that God was wating fo • them to give Him th-ir hearts and in re- turn He would give teem a gift at the Holy Spirit— the gift of strength. Appropriate hymns were slug Mr S. Woods presiding at the organ with his usual ability.•
